welcome:
You are a **Wanax**: a [[bronze|Bronze]] Age ruler of a people on the eastern shores of a great sea. Many of you share one world, and it keeps moving whether you are watching or not.

This Codex is the world's book of knowledge. Every article links onward — follow what you are curious about, or open it from the **?** on any drawer or notification to read about exactly what is in front of you.

## The opening dispatch {#welcome-your-opening-dispatch}

Open **Your people await you** in Notifications for your first steps, starting supplies and the world's pace. If you begin again after losing your realm, look for **Begin again**.

Your [[horde|Host]] lives on subsistence while you search for a home. Once you found a city, put people to work producing [[food]].

## Physical world rules {#welcome-three-rules-that-explain-almost-everything}

**Game days belong to the world.** The world advances one game day at a time, and every duration the game shows you counts in game days. See [[time]].

**The world runs without you.** Nobody pauses. Fields are worked, soldiers are paid and granaries fill and empty while you sleep. Plan your supplies and read [[coming-back|what happened while you were gone]].

**Command is never instant.** An order to an army in the field travels by Runner, a person who has to walk there. Until he arrives, the army does what it was last told. See [[runners]].

## First steps {#welcome-where-to-begin}

1. [[getting-in]] — joining a world.
2. [[horde]] — you start as a people on the move, not as a city.
3. [[founding]] — choosing a home.
4. [[screen]] — what every button on the screen does.
5. [[city]] and [[citizens]] — putting your people to work.
6. [[food]] — keeping your city fed.

Unfamiliar words are explained in the [[glossary]].

When something seems wrong, it may be a known [[rough-edges|rough edge]] — or worth a [[report]].

account:
Click your Wanax name at the top left to open **Account**. Its realm summary has five rows for your selected world: your Wanax name, founding game day, owned active cities, their total population, and your realm's [[kharis]].

**Since today 18:34**, or another clock time and date, marks the founding of your current life. If you have risen and started again, it follows that new life. A Host that has not founded its capital shows **Not yet founded**. The population is the population of your cities; it does not include your travelling Host. No other ruler's cities or statistics appear here.

From [[keryx]], use `keryx me`, or `keryx me --json`. The API is `GET /api/v1/worlds/{world}/me` with your Bearer token. It returns only your own realm in that world.

The same account window lets you change your password, open [[community-chat]], and sign out. To delete your account, write to the admin in the community chat.
screen:
The map, drawers and dispatches show your realm and let you give orders.

## The top bar {#screen-top-bar}

- **Your Wanax name**, on the left.
- **Dispatch chips** slide in when something happens. Click one to open it. **✕ all** clears the chips — they stay in the archive.
- **Date and the sun or moon** — the world's calendar ([[time]]).
- **☍** opens the Notifications archive, with a badge for unread events ([[coming-back]]).
- **⌕** opens search (also `f` or `/`): your cities, cities you can see, your armies, received letters and rumours. Search letters by their text or Wanax names, and rumours by text, region or category. Arrow keys move; Enter jumps to a map result or opens Letters/[[gossip]]. Letters come from your current inbox (up to 30), not a full correspondence archive; rumours come from the latest 30 items in the Gossip feed. Reopen search to refresh.
- **?** opens this Codex.

## The drawer bar {#screen-bottom-bar-the-drawers}

| | Drawer | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| 🏛 | **City** | One settlement: people, production, buildings, garrison — [[city]] |
| ⚔ | **War** | Forces, recruiting, armies in the field — [[units|Forces]] |
| ✉ | **Diplomacy** | Letters, [[trade|trade offers]], known cities and rulers — [[messengers]] |
| ⚖ | **Economy** | Goods across all cities, [[transfers|transfers]], [[routes|standing orders]] — [[goods]] |
| ⛩ | **Kult** | The [[gods|gods]] — [[kharis]] |
| ✎ | **Report** | Tell the builders something is wrong — [[report]] |

Every drawer has a **?** in its header that opens its article here.

## Map controls {#screen-the-map}

- **Left-click a hex** to look at it — the inspect panel opens on the right on a wide screen, titled by its ground. On a hex your own people work it also says how many workers are there and what they produce. A foreign city shows its owner and **Defence** says **Defended** when walls or land defenders are seen, or **No defenders seen** when both are known to be absent. **Unknown** means the defence data could not be read. You can still write a message or open **March here**.

- **Right-click a hex** to give an order there — the march menu opens ([[marching]]).

- On a touchscreen, drag with one finger to pan, tap a hex to inspect it, pinch with two fingers to zoom, and hold still briefly to open orders.

- Drag, or use WASD or the arrow keys, to pan. **+** and **−** zoom, **⌂** re-centres.

### Sound and mobile windows {#screen-the-map-2}

- **♫** silences all sound: the sign-in screen's opening theme, the music, the horn when troops receive a march order, the clash of a resolved [[battle|battle]], a short call when your forces arrive, and a soft chime for each new dispatch while you are playing.

- **⚒** toggles an activity overlay.

On mobile, windows fill the screen. Use the close button at the top right to return to the map. Opening another window closes the previous one.
runners:
**Command is never instant.** This is the rule that makes Megaron different from most strategy games.

When you tell a unit in the field to turn around, change course or change stance, you do not reach the unit — you send a **Runner**, a real person who must walk to it. The game gives the next meeting estimate, such as *"Runner following the unit — next meeting today 22:40."* Until then the unit keeps doing what it was last told.

## How orders travel {#runners-details}

While the Runner is still on the road, the order shows under the unit in **War → Forces** and in `keryx army`, with the next meeting time — it disappears once he has delivered it. If the unit moves again, the meeting estimate can change; it does not promise that the order is already delivered.

The one exception is your [[horde|Nomadic Host]]: you travel with it in person, so it obeys at once.

## Order travel and warning time {#runners-why-this-is-good-for-you}

Because orders move at walking pace, **a defender who is offline is not helpless.** An attacker has to cross ground you can see, and your answer usually has less ground to cross than his army does. Distance is the defender's ally. See [[defence]].

## Failed orders {#runners-when-an-order-fails}

Sometimes a Runner arrives and the order can no longer be carried out. You get an *Order failed* notification that names the order and the reason. Look at the unit in **War → Forces** and decide again.

Recall and redirect are sent from **War → Forces**, or — for redirect — by right-clicking a new destination for a unit that is already marching. See [[marching]].

## Catching a moving force {#runners-catching-up-with-a-moving-unit}

A unit on the march does not wait for its orders. A Runner sent to it — to recall it, redirect it or change its [[stances|stance]] — is aimed at the point on its road where he can **catch up** with it, and the game tells you when he will. Runners are quicker than soldiers, but not endlessly: a recall or redirect that cannot catch the unit before it arrives still sends a Runner to its destination. For a newly sent land order, a missed meeting is not the end of the journey: if the unit has moved again, the Runner keeps the order and follows it along a new physical route. March, recall, redirect and stance orders take effect only when the Runner and the unit actually meet. The pending order says when its next meeting is expected and when it is following a new route. If it must wait before it can continue, the pending order says so without promising a delivery time. A Runner cannot deliver to a destroyed unit or one you no longer own.

### Sacred letters and order Runners {#runners-catching-up-with-a-moving-unit-2}

Letters to other Wanaxes travel the same way, but they are sacred and cannot be stopped: see [[messengers]].

## Runners crossing water {#runners-crossing-the-sea}

A Runner whose road to your unit crosses open water cannot swim it — it waits in your own port for a ship — anyone's — to sail that way, the same as a letter does. See [[sea]] for how the crossing works, and what happens if the ship carrying it is lost.

## The Runners tab {#runners-the-runners-tab}

**Diplomacy → Runners** (or `keryx runners`) shows every runner of yours that is still out, in groups: **waiting for a ship**, **on the way**, **aboard a ship**, **waiting for an answer**, and **on the way home**. A waiting runner says where it stands, since when, and why — and offers **Arrange passage** (one of your own free ships) or **Call back** (only when it waits in your own port). A runner **waiting for an answer** has reached the other Wanax's city and stands there until they answer — the tab says since when, and when it heads home if nobody does. An order's runner names the order it carries. Times are the clock time something happens — "today 18:34" — never a game day count.

The tab also lists other Wanaxes' runners, but only where you can know they are there: standing in one of your cities or ports, or aboard one of your ships. You see whose runner it is and where — never what it carries, and never the road it came by. Runners are sacred; a ship's captain does not read the letters. See [[messengers]] and [[sea]].

## Runner speed {#runners-runner-speed}

On land a Runner needs half a foot army's [[terrain|terrain]] time ([[marching]]). At an
ordinary [[rivers|river]] crossing he uses the ship's river cost; at a [[river-ford|ford]] he wades.
At sea he has no separate speed: he travels with the real ship carrying him.

A runner follows a saved land route one province at a time, including the walk to a harbour and the walk after landing. It sees from each province when it reaches it, and remembers that ground even while you are away. Runners remain sacred: they cannot be intercepted.

## Arranging a ship for a Runner {#arrange-passage}

Waiting for a ship to happen to sail the right way is not your only choice. From your **outbox** (Diplomacy, or `keryx outbox`), a runner waiting for passage shows an **Arrange passage** button (or `keryx passage`) whenever one of your own ships qualifies — the choice of ship is always yours to make, but only real, eligible ships are ever offered: a [[galley]] or [[emporos]] (never a [[war-galley]]), standing free in port with no mission of its own.

- **Sending one out:** the ship must stand in the SAME port the runner is waiting in. It sails straight for the runner's destination, boards it the moment it leaves, and puts it ashore there — no different from boarding any ship that happened to be going that way, except this one you chose yourself.

### Fetching a waiting Runner home {#arrange-passage-2}

- **Bringing one home:** a runner that has finished its errand and is waiting in a **foreign** port may be fetched instead — any of your own ports will do. The ship sails there, waits (**War → Forces** shows it "waiting at (…) for the runner's return", or `keryx unit` says the same), and carries the runner all the way home the moment it is ready to travel.

- Either way, **the ship still finishes its own mission on its own** afterwards — it always sails home again, exactly like Land, Patrol or Explore. The runner never commands the ship; you send the ship for the runner, never the other way round. While it sails out, the drawer and `keryx unit` show it "carrying a runner to (…)".

- The ship's own risks are unchanged: it can still be damaged, captured or sunk, and a starved crew still turns it for home ([[upkeep]]) — none of that touches the runner, who stands safely ashore the whole time.

## A runner lost at sea {#runner-lost-at-sea}

A [[storms|storm]] can sink a runner's ship. If a ship sinks in [[battle|battle]] and no enemy ship survives to rescue the runner, the runner is lost too. This applies to [[messengers|letters]], [[trade|trade offers]] and [[runners|orders]].

If the crew disappears from [[upkeep|hunger or desertion]], the runner steps ashore if it can reach a nearby settlement. Out at sea, with no way to leave, it is lost.

You learn immediately that **your own runner was lost**. This is the one exception to news needing a physical bearer. The dispatch tells you nothing else about the battle or other people’s ships.

### The lost Runner’s sealed contents {#runner-lost-at-sea-details}

Open the dispatch to read the whole sealed contents: the letter and any reply, the trade proposal or the order, its recorded departure time (for example, "Sent yesterday 18:34"), and its origin and destination. The record does not change when cities or orders change later.

A lost runner cannot deliver the message later. Sending again is your decision. If another ship rescues it, see [[runner-rescued-at-sea]].

An older sealed record may have no preserved departure game day; it says "Sent on an unknown game day" rather than guessing.

The dispatch names people first: "From you, at Mycenae, to Wanax Oledoledoff at Tiryns." An order names "your [[elite-infantry]] at (9, 4)" instead. The recipient's public Wanax name, your unit's name and the places are preserved when the runner is lost; later name changes do not rewrite the sealed record. Account logins are not used.

### Reading a Runner loss report {#runner-lost-at-sea-details-2}

The headline names only the recipient: "Your runner to Wanax Oledoledoff at Tiryns was lost at sea in a storm." For an order: "Your runner to your Bronze Guard at (9, 4) was lost at sea in a storm." The full origin stays in the sealed envelope below.

## Passage aboard a ship {#runner-passage}

A [[messengers|letter]] or a [[runners|Runner]] carrying your order cannot swim, and it never guesses at a crossing — it needs a real ship, full stop. When its road crosses open water:

- It runs to **your own nearest coastal or harboured city** and waits there — you are told which one, and why. If you have no coastal or harboured city anywhere, the message is refused outright at the moment you send it, rather than dispatched to wait forever.

### Boarding any suitable ship {#runner-passage-2}

- The moment **any** ship or trade route — yours or another Wanax's — sails from that port toward the right side of the sea, it **boards** — free, no cargo space taken — and steps off wherever that ship lands, then finishes the trip on foot. Runners are sacred: every captain takes them aboard, even between Wanaxes at war. It only boards a ship that lands it **nearer its goal** than the port it waits in — a ship bound the wrong way, it lets sail. The runner never changes where the ship goes, and the ship's owner sees only that a runner of yours is aboard, never what it carries.

- A storm can [[runner-lost-at-sea|lose the runner]]. In battle a surviving enemy ship [[runner-rescued-at-sea|rescues it]]; a captured ship keeps it aboard. It leaves that actual ship in its next port and continues. A damaged ship that survives takes its runner home to the next port, without sealing or loss.

### Waiting for a sailing {#runner-passage-3}

- If no ship sails that way for a while, it simply keeps waiting — nothing crosses on its own. See "A runner stuck waiting" below for what you can do about it.

None of this changes anything for a message or order whose road stays on dry land — a Runner on land never needs a ship, only [[marching|the roads]] it can already walk (a river still needs a ford or a boat of its own, unrelated to sea passage).

## Passage markers on the map {#runner-passage-on-map}

Your own [[messengers|letter]] or [[runners|Runner]] is drawn exactly where it really is, not sailing on its own across open water:

- **Waiting** — it stands still in the port it ran to, a gold pennant marking it as yours. A small red mark on top means a **PassageStalled** dispatch has already fired for this wait.
- **Aboard** — it rides the deck of whichever ship or trade route picked it up, moving exactly when and where that ship does. Hover it to see the carrier's name.
- **Ashore** — once the ship lands it, it steps off and finishes the last stretch on foot, same as any Runner on land.
- **No word** — after a rescue its location is unknown to you: no marker, carrier name or sight. It tells you about the detour only when it physically comes home. Sealed markers remain a recovery measure for older unresolved journeys.

## A runner rescued at sea {#runner-rescued-at-sea}

A herald is sacred. When its ship sinks in battle, a surviving enemy ship takes the runner aboard. A captured ship also keeps its runner safe, even though its owner has changed. The new owner cannot read the sealed message or hold the runner captive.

The runner follows that **actual ship to its next port**, steps ashore and continues toward the original destination. It may need to wait for another passage. A damaged ship that survives and turns home keeps its runner aboard until that home port; that is neither a loss nor a rescue.

### Rescue and the next physical port {#runner-rescued-at-sea-details}

You receive no instant rescue news or location. Your outbox says **no word**, and the runner's unknown position gives you no map marker or sight. The recipient simply receives the message later.

The report says when the runner came home, such as "Home today 18:34". When the runner comes home with its answer, it brings its own account of the rescue ship and the port where it landed. A one-way order runner does not send a report home from afar. Only [[runner-lost-at-sea|loss]] is reported immediately. See [[sea]] and [[messengers]].

The account names the ship and the actual towns in a sentence: "Home today 18:34. Your runner was rescued at sea by the Sacred Dolphin and put ashore at Tiryns, then went ashore at Mycenae." With only one landing: "Home today 18:34. Your runner was rescued at sea by the Sacred Dolphin and put ashore at Tiryns." The town names are preserved when the runner steps ashore.

## Calling a Runner home {#runner-return}

In **Diplomacy → Correspondence**, use **Call it back** on the waiting runner's row, or use the same choice in its **PassageStalled** dispatch. In Keryx, find the runner with `outbox`, then use `call-back --id <messenger-id>`.

This works only for an outbound runner waiting for a ship in **your own port**. A runner already aboard a ship, or waiting in a foreign port on its return journey, cannot be called back this way — arrange passage instead.

The runner turns around and walks home over land, delivering nothing. The confirmation tells you when it will return; it is still travelling until then. A letter comes home undelivered, and an order comes home withdrawn.

## A Runner awaiting passage {#runner-waiting}

Wait long enough with no ship sailing the right way, and you get a **PassageStalled** dispatch: the runner, the port it's standing in, where it's trying to reach, and the ships (if any) of yours already there. Nothing forces your hand — it keeps waiting exactly where it is until you act, and the dispatch only ever fires once per spell of waiting (a later known waiting spell can trigger it again; an unknown rescued runner sends no news from a foreign port). Three choices:

- **Arrange passage** — the same button as above, right there in the dispatch.
- **Call it back** — give up on this errand and bring the runner home undelivered. See the instructions below.
- **Let it wait** — close the dispatch and do nothing. It keeps waiting, exactly as it was.
coming-back:
While you were away, the world kept moving. Here is how to catch up.

## The Notifications archive {#coming-back-open-the-notifications-archive}

It is a permanent record of everything that happened to you — there is deliberately no "clear all". Urgent events are marked. Critical food warnings and a garrison’s latest hunger warning appear first. When that city’s recovery arrives, its old hunger warning returns to its place in history. Each notification shows when it happened using your clock and date, such as **yesterday 14:05**. If its time cannot be established, it says **time unavailable**.

Click any row to open it in the **Dispatch window**. The same window opens from a dispatch chip in the top bar. It gives you:

### Following a dispatch to its place {#coming-back-open-the-notifications-archive-2}

- what happened,
- **⌖ Take me there**, which jumps the map to where it happened,
- on a letter or a trade offer, **✉ Reply** instead, which opens your letters with that Wanax (in Keryx: `keryx letters <id>`, printed under the notice),
- **? Read about this**, which opens the Codex article that explains it,
- a checkbox, *Stop these as dispatches*. Muting only silences the chip. The event is always kept in the archive. In [[keryx|Keryx]] the same setting is `keryx dispatches --mute <Kind>`, and it is shared between the two.

## Priorities after time away {#coming-back-what-to-act-on-first}

1. **Food** — a [[food|shortfall]] kills people every game day it lasts.
2. **Pay and bread** — [[upkeep]] warnings mean soldiers need [[silver|silver]] or food. Soldiers share [[grain|grain]], [[fish|fish]] and [[oil|oil]] with the people, but their meals are itemized separately. Produce more food or send a [[transfers|transfer]]. A notice marks when garrison hunger starts and when it ends.
3. **Foreign marches** — someone is coming, and you know roughly when. See [[defence]].
4. **Sieges and occupation** — a clock is running on a city. See [[sieges]] and [[occupation]].

A [[kharis|Kharis]] notice marks each change between Favorable, Indifferent, Suspicious and Wrathful. Check **Kult** for Kharis and the upkeep of the cult. It fades from the start; every active city and its residents count toward the cost. A warning marks a fall below 30 with negative net; below 15 punishment can fall, with or without a temple. An actual punishment protects you for seven game days; Kult shows when this protection ends. Staff and feed temples, then check the projected net.

Then look at **City → Production** for idle [[citizens]], and **Diplomacy → Correspondence** to ask a contacted Wanax about [[trade]].

## Preparing to leave your realm {#coming-back-making-the-next-absence-easier}

Set up [[routes|standing orders]] for food and materials, keep [[food|food]] in the city’s stores, and post a [[stances|watch]] where enemies would come from.

Historical food reserve releases, food support reports and food reserve warnings are grouped at the end of Notifications. Choose **show reports** to read them; **All notifications** returns to the archive. Rumours you have heard are mixed into the same list, each marked **Rumour**.
horde:
You do not begin with a city. You begin as a **Nomadic Host** — a whole people on the move, standing as one token on the map. There is no separate founding screen: the map is the game from the first second.

Find it (the map centres on you) and **left-click the hex it stands on**. The inspect panel opens, headed *Nomadic Host*.

## The Host’s people and escort {#horde-what-the-host-is}

- **A thousand people**, and they are the city you will found — its starting population, not soldiers. <!-- src: api/handlers/nomadic_host.go nomadicHostPopulation -->
- **Two cohorts of [[spearmen|spearmen]] escort you.** They live on [[grain|grain]] and draw no [[silver|silver]] pay, just like settled spearmen.
- **The Host itself eats nothing.** A people on the move carries its own bread. The grain in the store is a dowry that goes into your city's stores the game day you found.
- **The Host cannot fight.** The escort can.
- **It sees two hexes** (further across open water or towards mountains) — exactly the ground a settlement would work. Wherever the Host stands, it can see the whole [[catchment]] it would get by stopping there.

## Moving the Nomadic Host {#horde-walking}

**Right-click any hex** to open the order menu, pick the Host and press **March →** — or left-click a hex and use **March here →** in the inspect panel. The Host moves at 90% of Spearmen's speed and reveals the map as it goes.

Unlike everything else you will ever command, **the Host obeys instantly**: you are walking with it. See [[runners]] for what comes after.

## Inspecting the Host’s current ground {#horde-where-you-are}

The Host's marker, sight and founding place follow the Province it physically occupies, including during a march. Its hover and panel say **Marching**, **Waiting** (with the reason this ground cannot be settled), or **Can found here**. Click the marker's current hex to open the Host panel. Keryx `founding status` and `status` show the same position and state.

You can found on valid ground while the Host is marching. The city rises where the Host stands when you confirm, and the Host disappears. If it has moved from the place you confirmed, the order is refused; reopen its panel and read the new site before founding.

## The Host’s founding reserves {#horde-reserves-for-founding}

Before founding, the Host lives on subsistence and its reserves do not drain. A new Host carries **120 silver**; a Host rising after losing every city starts with **60 silver**. Its grain and silver go into your city when you settle. Your [[welcome|opening dispatch]] records what your Host carries. Choose your site for its food, resources and position.

When you have found your place: [[founding]].
founding:
Founding your first city — the **metropolis** — is the one decision in Megaron you cannot undo. The Host dissolves forever.

## Choosing founding ground {#founding-read-the-ground-first}

The [[horde|Host]] panel shows the [[terrain|terrain]] and four short assessments for the hex you stand on: **Feeds itself: yes/no**, **[[timber]]: yes/no**, **[[stone]]: yes/no**, and **Ships: yes / never — inland**. An inland metropolis can never build a harbour or ships ([[buildings]]). They use the existing forecast for known ground; unknown means the forecast is unavailable. The [[catchment]] you would claim glows on the map. Open **Details** for the full founding forecast, deposits, production, gifts, each catchment hex, and the Host’s people and supplies. It updates as you walk.

Under **Details**, the forecast gives the [[grain|grain]] your fields would produce against what your people would eat, and one of three verdicts:

- **It feeds itself** — the fields cover the mouths with room to spare.
- **Marginal** — positive but thin. Draft one cohort and you are eating into the food stock.
- **It does not feed itself** — you are told how many game days your carried grain buys, and whether a [[farm]] would fix it. If it says a farm will not help, there is no farmable ground in reach at all.

### Founding deposits and food risk {#founding-read-the-ground-first-2}

The gap between *marginal* and *does not feed itself* has killed more young cities than any war. See [[food]].

In **Details**, below the grain line, look for **deposits**: [[copper|copper]], [[tin|tin]], [[silver|silver]], [[cedar|cedar]]. A site with metal under it is worth walking extra game days for. A site with none is not a mistake — you can buy metal ([[trade]]) — but you will be buying it from someone who walked those game days. Read [[bronze]] before you decide.

## Where founding is forbidden {#founding-where-you-cannot-found}

Not on sea, mountain, [[rivers|river]] or [[semi-desert|semi-desert]], and **not within two hexes of another settlement** — city centres stand at least **three** hexes apart. Closer than that, the game refuses and tells you how far to move. At three or more your [[catchment]] may share ground with a neighbour's; who works a shared hex is told in [[catchment]].

## Settling the Nomadic Host {#founding-settling}

The Host panel follows its current physical position, including on the march. **Waiting** explains why the current ground cannot be settled; **Can found here** means the site is valid. If the Host has moved while you were confirming, reopen the panel before trying again.

Press **⚒ Found the metropolis here** at the bottom of the Host panel. Read the warning beside the button, then press **Found the metropolis** to confirm. **Keep travelling** closes the warning without founding. In exchange:

### A new city’s starting stores {#founding-settling-2}

- The Host's people become your city's population.
- Everything carried — grain and silver — pours into the city. A new city starts with **no timber and no stone**: its [[catchment]] needs ground that produces these materials (or a neighbour to buy from) before the first building can rise.
- Forces standing on the hex become its garrison.
- **Demeter's gift**: found inland, with farmable ground in your catchment, and a Farm appears, free.
- **Poseidon's gift**: found on the coast and a [[galley|galley]] is waiting in the harbour — instead of the farm. The sea feeds a harbour city; a gift is one or the other, never both.
- Your first [[citizens]] are placed on the best food land automatically, until the city feeds itself — and always at least one, so even a [[colonies|colony]] of 100 has someone in the fields. The rest stand idle, waiting for you.

Next: [[city]].

### Founding food and timber forecasts {#founding-settling-3}

The forecast lists grain and [[fish|fish]] production separately from the population's full food consumption. A production deficit uses up carried grain before hunger begins. Fish counts as food. Hunger begins only when daily meals are not fully covered, after stored grain, fish, [[oil|oil]], [[wine|wine]] and emergency [[livestock|livestock]] have been used. A production deficit warns of future hunger once reserves run out; it does not by itself mean the population is starving.

If the known catchment has no timber or cedar to cover timber costs, the forecast warns before you found. Unknown ground may still hold wood; scout it or plan deliveries. A fully known catchment without wood needs imports for building.

Place citizens on [[olive-grove|olive groves]], [[maquis|maquis]], [[hills|hills]] or river valleys for timber, or on [[cedar-forest|cedar forest]] for cedar to cover timber costs, and on stone-bearing ground for stone; idle citizens produce nothing. Maquis, hills and river valleys each have one timber place before a [[lumbermill]] is built, yielding 0.33 timber per worker per game day ([[catchment]]). The forecast says when Demeter’s farm is already included; another farm is not an extra founding gift.

### Farms on grain-bearing hills {#founding-settling-4}

On grain-bearing hills, a Farm at level 1 makes 0.85 grain per worker per game day, with room for five workers. Plain hills give 0.5 per worker. With another grain-bearing hill in reach, six food workers can feed a new city of 1,000 people; leave the rest for timber and stone. Check the forecast for your actual site.
last-city:
When your last city falls, to [[food|hunger]], to a conqueror's annexation or to fire, your reign in it is over. The screen that follows tells the story of that reign, from the city's rise to its fall. Under the story you choose what comes next.

## Refounding after losing your last city {#last-city-gather-the-survivors}

Survivors set out again as a small [[horde|Nomadic Host]]:

- **Between 400 and 800 people.** The number falls as it falls. <!-- src: api/handlers/rise.go risenHostMinGubbar/risenHostMaxGubbar -->
- **One company of [[spearmen|spearmen]]** as escort, where a newcomer has two.
- **60 [[silver|silver]]**, a fixed reserve; the spearman escort draws no silver pay. Bread for the road is the same as a newcomer carries.
- **Another shore.** Refugees do not stay where the enemy stands. The Host is set down on another landmass, or on an island, wherever there is free ground.

Until you found a city, your Host stands under [[gods|the gods]]' protection: anyone who attacks it loses 70 [[kharis|kharis]]. See [[xenia]].

Everything you knew stays yours: your letters, the cities you have [[contact|made contact with]] and the map you have seen. Then it is [[founding]] again, as at the very start.

## Leaving a world {#last-city-leave-this-world}

You leave this world for good and cannot rise in it again. **Your account remains**, and the next world is open to you. To delete the account itself, write to the admin in the [[community-chat|community chat]].

In [[keryx|Keryx]] the same two choices are `keryx rise` and `keryx leave`.

See also: [[occupation]] and [[sieges]], for how a city is lost, and [[xenia]] for the gods' order among the Wanaxes.
city:
**Left-click your own city** and the City drawer opens on it. If you hold several settlements, the **‹** and **›** arrows in the header cycle between them; your capital is marked **★**.

The drawer has three tabs: **Production**, **Buildings** and **Garrison**. If your city is under siege, a red banner at the top names who holds the approaches ([[sieges]]).

## Production — the dashboard

Three sections show the essentials:

- **Population** — whole citizen groups, those free to work, and [[livestock|livestock]]. One citizen represents 100 people; fewer than 100 remaining people do not make a free worker. The exact population is under **More**.
- **[[catchment]] & workplaces** — the placement grid, where you put people to work. See [[citizens]].
- **Food** — how many game days the city’s current [[grain|grain]], [[fish|fish]] and [[oil|oil]] stocks last at current consumption, whether stocks are growing, and whether the fields can feed everyone. See [[food]].

Open **More** for people in service and the labour pool, **Devotion** ([[temples]]), **Food details** ([[food]]), **Last game day**, and **Daily history → Show recent game days**.

## Buildings

What stands, what is queued (with a **✕** to cancel), forces in training, and **Construct**. See [[buildings]].

## Garrison

The forces standing in this city. Orders to them are given from **War** ([[units|Forces]]).
catchment:
A settlement lives off the land around it. That land is its **catchment**: the city's own hex plus the ring of hexes within **two** steps of it — eighteen hexes of land and water that its people can work. <!-- src: internal/hexgrid CatchmentRadius -->

The catchment is the **only** place production comes from. There is no abstract "income": every sack of [[grain|grain]], every log and every ingot was produced by one of your [[citizens]] standing on one of these hexes, or working in a [[buildings|building]] in the city.

## Catchment reach and shared ground {#catchment-details}

**[[maquis|Maquis]], [[hills|hills]] and [[rivers|river]] valleys also give [[timber|timber]]:** each hex has room for one timber worker, producing **0.33 timber per game day**. A [[buildings|Lumbermill]] adds four places, making room for five timber workers, and multiplies each worker's output by ×1.7 at level 1, ×2.4 at level 2 or ×3.1 at level 3. Olive groves remain a richer source of timber; [[cedar-forest|cedar forest]] produces [[cedar|cedar]], which can cover timber costs.

On the map, a city's catchment is outlined in gold when you have that city in focus: when its City drawer is open, or when you click the city itself.

## Catchment resources and blockades {#catchment-what-it-means-for-you}

- **Where you found decides what you can make.** A catchment of [[plains|plains]] and coast feeds people; one with a mountain may hold [[copper|copper]] or [[silver|silver]]. The [[founding]] forecast shows you the catchment before you commit.

- **Neighbours share ground.** Cities may be founded as close as **three** hexes apart, so their catchments overlap. A hex belongs to whichever city has [[citizens]] working on it; a neighbour cannot place anyone there while you hold it.

- **A held hex can be taken.** Stand one of your own forces on it in [[stances|fortify or sentry]], then place a citizen there. The holder's citizens go home to their idle pool, their building on the hex becomes yours at the same level, and any build they had queued there is cancelled and refunded. They are told by dispatch. A unit that merely marches through takes nothing, and if the holder has a unit standing guard there too, you must defeat it first ([[battle]]).

- **They can take it back** the same way: a unit in fortify or sentry, then a citizen placed.

### Unscouted and shared workplaces {#catchment-what-it-means-for-you-2}

- **A hex you have not scouted cannot be worked.** It is listed below the grid rather than drawn.

- **An enemy on your catchment hurts.** A hostile unit in [[stances|sentry]] on one of your hexes stops that hex feeding you. Hold enough of them long enough and a city falls without a battle — see [[sieges]].

A hex shown as held by another city is already being worked by that city. Shared reach does not make its workers yours; the placement card explains whether you can take it.
citizens:
**One citizen marker stands for one hundred people.** A city of a thousand gives you ten. Each citizen stands on **one hex, or in one building, producing one good**. That is the whole labour model.

## Placing citizens {#citizens-placing-people}

Open **City → Production → Catchment & workplaces**. You get a hex diagram: the centre hex labelled **City**, ringed by your [[catchment]]. Each ring hex shows its number and how many goods it can produce.

**Click a hex** and a row appears for each good it can produce, with:

- what it makes now and what **the next citizen would add**,
- occupancy as dots — filled for placed citizens, hollow for free places,
- or simply **full** when the hex is at its limit.

Each row has **+1**, **Fill** and **−1**. *Fill* keeps adding until the hex is full or your idle people run out. If a placement is refused, the reason appears in red under the rows; the hex stays selected so you can try another good.

**Click the centre City hex** to staff [[buildings]] — same rows, same buttons.

## The next citizen’s production {#citizens-the-one-number-that-matters}

The *next citizen would add* figure is all you need for a good decision. A citizen placed past a hex's limit produces nothing, which is why the row says **full** instead of letting you find out slowly. Every good has a limit on that hex; a relevant building adds four places and raises each worker's output.

## Free citizens and new population {#free-citizens}

Your first citizens are placed on the best food land when you [[founding|found]]. Afterwards, each time the population crosses another hundred, the new citizen remains **free to work** until you place it. Choose a hex or the central City hex and assign that citizen to a job. Keep enough citizens producing food as your city [[growth|grows]].

Idle citizens are wasted citizens. So are citizens producing something nobody uses — see [[surplus]].

On the map, a small marker shows the hexes where your people are at work.

[[fish]] feeds your people just as [[grain|grain]] does. A city living on stored food is still fed. Hunger begins only when the daily meal remains short after the [[food|feeding chain]] has been exhausted; see [[growth]].

One placeable **citizen represents 100 people**. Population counts people; City and Goods count these citizens. The food-workers estimate assumes the best grain and fish slots for the population. Moving workers may require rearranging the remaining food placements; the army draws from the same food stocks, as shown separately in the food balance.

### Food from fractional citizens {#free-citizens-2}

People outside whole groups of 100 automatically produce a fraction of the best food worker’s output: 42 people give 42 hundredths. They make grain or fish, whichever their best food hex produces most of, including its building bonus. This work is invisible and takes no place from your citizens. Nearby ground supplies its grain separately. City food details show these automatic contributions beside the placed citizens needed for meals. The count uses production rather than stored food; it is an estimate for the best food slots, not a recommendation to remove particular citizens.

[[temple]] workers use the same citizen pool as other jobs. Use `keryx staff temple +1` to assign one, `staff temple -1` to free one (with several temples, add `--god <god>`), and `roster` to see their assignments. See [[temples]].
fishing:
[[fish]] feeds your people just like [[grain|grain]] ([[food]]). Place [[citizens]] on a fishing hex in **City**, or use `keryx place fish <hex> +1`. The available places and the next citizen’s output come from that city’s current production options.

| Water | Fishing places | Fish per fisher per game day |
|---|---|---|
| Coastal water | 2 | 1 |
| Bay | 2 | 2 |
| Deep water | 0, 1, 2 or 4 at harbour levels 0, 1, 2 or 3 | 1 |

## Fishing places, bays and storms {#fishing-details}

A **bay** is [[coastal-sea|coastal water]] with land on at least four of its six sides. Rivers and [[river-ford|fords]] count as land for this rule; coastal water, deep water and the Thalassa do not. A missing hex beyond the map edge does not count as land. A bay doubles each fisher’s catch; it has the same two places as other coastal water.

Deep-water fishing requires the city’s [[harbour]]. The harbour supplies deep-water places without multiplying the catch. It adds no places or production to coastal water or bays. Rivers and fords keep their own fishing places and production.

A harbour creates places, not workers. Put citizens on the deep-water hexes to use them. Higher harbour levels open more places there, while each fisher still catches 1 fish per game day.

**A storm stops the fishing.** While a [[storms|storm]] stands on a fishing hex, the fishers stay placed there but catch nothing. They fish again the game day it has moved on. **City** shows *Storm over N fishing grounds*, and `keryx city` and `keryx status` print the same line: *its fishers stay but catch nothing while it stands*.

## Deep-water fishing {#deep-water-fishing}

A harbour stands in the city and opens fishing places on **every deep-water hex in its [[catchment]]**. Build it through **City → Buildings → Construct**, or `keryx build --type harbour`. The city must meet the coast rule described in [[buildings]].

| Harbour level | Fishing places on each deep-water hex |
|---|---|
| No harbour | 0 |
| Level 1 | 1 |
| Level 2 | 2 |
| Level 3 | 4 |

Each deep-water fisher catches **1 fish per game day**, at every harbour level. The harbour has no fishing multiplier and adds no coastal places. Coastal water always has two places producing 1 fish per fisher per game day; a bay has two places producing 2 each. See [[fishing]] for the bay rule. Rivers and fords receive no harbour bonus.

The harbour has no city workplaces to staff. Place your [[citizens]] on the deep-water hexes themselves. Its role in sea trade is separate from fishing. A [[shipyard|Shipyard]] is a separate building for building and repairing [[sea|ships]].

## Shipyard workers {#shipyard-workers}

**An unstaffed shipyard stands still; one worker keeps it working.**

You can pay for an order while the shipyard is unstaffed. It waits with **“waiting for shipyard workers”** and has no ready time. Removing the last worker pauses every build and repair; completed work and paid materials are kept. Staff the shipyard again to resume the remaining work and see a new ready time.

Work already under way when this rule takes effect keeps its remaining work. Workers are not assigned automatically.

See [[citizens|Citizens and placement]], [[units|Soldiers and ships]] and [[sea|The Thalassa]].

growth:
A city grows when it has a **surplus of food** — when it produces more food each game day than its people eat. Growing costs no food: the surplus stays in the same city [[grain|grain]], [[fish|fish]] and [[oil|oil]] stocks that feed your people.

- **Surplus, not store.** What counts is the daily balance — grain, fish and oil produced, minus what the people eat — shown as the food *net* on the city. A positive net grows the city; zero or below holds it steady, even with full stores.

- **Rate.** A fed city with a positive net grows by **0.5% of its people per game day** (at least one person), before the variety bonus below. A city of 1 000 gains about 5 a game day.

- **Surplus size.** A bigger surplus fills your stores faster; it does not itself raise the growth rate. <!-- src: server/internal/economy/population_growth.go PopulationGrowthRatePerTick -->

## Growth from food surplus {#growth-details}

- **Variety.** Any of the food goods feeds people. Growth gains 10% per extra kind that forms at least **10% of the meal** eaten that game day, up to the existing variety ceiling: two substantial kinds give a 1.1 multiplier and four give 1.3. [[livestock]] counts only if eaten as a real share of emergency food. A good merely sitting in store, or eaten only in crumbs, gives no variety bonus.

- **Size.** The city's walls set its ceiling: 2 000 people with no wall, then 5 000, 10 000 and 20 000 for a Palisade, [[stone]] [[walls]] and [[bronze|Bronze]] Wall ([[buildings]]). Growth runs at its full rate right up to the ceiling and then stops; a city at its ceiling never shrinks because of it. The city screen says "Walls hold N", and `keryx status` says it too.

### When population growth stops {#growth-details-2}

In short: a city grows only while it makes more food than it eats; it holds steady when it does not; and it shrinks when it goes hungry. The city screen and `keryx status` say which of the three it is, and the food net behind it, for example "not growing: food net -1.7 per game day (needs more than 0)".

More people eat more, so a growing city eats into its own surplus until the balance reaches zero and growth stops — unless you put the new citizens to work on food.

Each time the population crosses another hundred, a new [[citizens|citizen]] becomes **free to work**. Choose its job yourself.

More people means more workers, more recruits and more mouths. See [[food]].

## The next free citizen {#growth-next-citizen}

Under **Citizens**, the City screen shows ten solid steps toward your next
citizen and the exact progress out of 100 people. For example, **64 / 100** means
36 more people are needed for the next citizen you can place. The estimated wait
uses the city's current growth, including food variety and the room inside its
walls. Game days appear with a real-time estimate from your world's clock;
when one game day or less remains, it says **next game day**.

The estimate changes with your city. A city with no growth says **not growing**;
at its population ceiling, **the walls are full**; during hunger, **shrinking**.
Keryx `city` and `status` show the same progress and explanation.
buildings:

Open **City → Buildings**. The tab shows what is **built** (and its level), the **build queue** (with an ETA and a **✕** to cancel), **training** (forces in progress) and **Construct**. Choose from the Construct list — each entry names the building and its cost — and press **+ Build**. A notification tells you when it is done.

### Walls, population and coastal access {#buildings-details-3}

**The wall is the ceiling.** A city with no wall holds 2 000 people, a Palisade 5 000, a [[walls|Stone Wall]] 10 000, a [[bronze|Bronze]] Wall 20 000. A city at its ceiling loses no one; it simply stops growing until you raise the wall. Each wall needs a [[granary]] of the same level first — Construct shows the next wall greyed out with "needs a Granary of level 2" until you have it. See [[growth]].

**The coast rule.** A city can build a Harbour or a Shipyard only if its own hex borders the sea or a [[rivers|river]]; an inland city never can, so to reach the sea you must found a coastal colony ([[colonies]]). The [[founding]] forecast tells you which kind of site you are looking at.

## Buildings on catchment hexes {#hex-buildings}

**[[farm]], [[mine]], [[lumbermill]] and [[stone-quarry]] stand on a hex, not in the city.** When you build one of these four, you choose which hex in your [[catchment]] it goes on, and it only ever helps that one hex. You may build more than one of the same kind — two Farms on two different [[grain|grain]] hexes each raise their own hex's cap, independently. A Mine's hex decides what it produces: build it on a [[copper|copper]], [[tin|tin]] or [[silver|silver]] deposit and it works that deposit; there is no separate building for silver.

**One building per hex.** A hex that already has one of these four — yours, or a neighbouring city's on a hex you share — cannot take another. Building the same kind again on its own hex raises its level.

### City buildings and Harbour reach {#hex-buildings-2}

Every other building, including **Harbour**, stands in the city itself. Harbour is the one exception worth naming: though it stands in the city (and needs the city's own hex to border the sea), its fishing effect reaches every deep-sea hex in your catchment at once. Harbour levels 1, 2 and 3 open 1, 2 and 4 places per deep-water hex; each fisher catches 1 [[fish|fish]] per game day. It gives no fishing multiplier or extra coastal places. See [[fishing]] and [[harbour]].

## Hex building production {#hex-production-buildings}

A farm, mine, lumbermill or stonequarry makes **space for four more workers** on its hex. Each of these buildings multiplies the hex's own **production** per worker: ×1.7 at level 1, ×2.4 at level 2, ×3.1 at level 3. Silver can only be mined with a mine — without one a silver deposit gives nothing. Olive press, winery and foundry work inside the city as before.

## Building upgrades and materials {#building-levels}

Buildings level up to three. **A higher level makes every worker on the hex produce more** — see the rule above.

A temple is built for a god: Construct lists one row per god (`keryx build --type temple --god potnia`), and building that god's temple again raises it. Building the same building again raises it by one level; for a hex building, choose the same hex. **Levels 2 and 3 of a Harbour, Shipyard or [[temple]]** also need **[[cedar|cedar]]**, which is scarce and often only available by [[trade]].

A building costs what it is made of: **[[timber|timber]]** for the Farm, [[market]], [[stable]], Harbour, Shipyard and Palisade; **[[stone|stone]]** for the Stone Quarry, Mine, [[barracks]], Temple and Stone Wall. The prices are shown live in Construct. If you are short of timber, your **cedar** pays the difference one for one — in buildings, ships and [[war-chariot|chariots]] alike.

Production workplaces need people assigned to them. The market has no workplaces and needs no workers; former market workers are free to assign elsewhere, with no population lost. Staff a workplace from the centre **City** hex of the placement grid ([[citizens]]).

### Construction queues and hex selectors {#building-levels-2}

If cancelling a queued build is refused, the reason appears in the Buildings tab.

The construction queue has a fixed limit, shown in `keryx build --queue`; population and building upgrades do not add slots. Finish or cancel a queued building before starting another when it is full. Hex buildings use `place`, not `staff`: for a lumbermill use `keryx place timber <hex> +2` (cedar on a cedar hex). `build --hex` accepts coordinates such as `3,-1` or the City ordinal `6`/`#6`.

## Demolishing a finished building {#demolition}

A finished building can be torn down so its hex or slot is free for something else. In the Buildings tab press **Demolish** beside the building and confirm; with keryx, `keryx demolish --hex 3,-1` for a hex building or `keryx demolish --type market` for a city one. Only your own city's buildings can be demolished.

The place is free at once — the new building then takes its normal time to build ([[catchment]] has the one-building-per-hex rule). **Nothing is refunded**, and anyone working in the building or on the places it made is lifted off and goes idle; they are not lost, and you can place them again ([[citizens]]). A hex keeps its base places, so a demolished farm's field still holds its first workers. A silver deposit gives nothing without its mine, so everyone mining it goes idle.

A temple also costs **10 [[kharis|kharis]] per level**, down to 1. The confirmation shows the actual loss and any lowered ceiling; existing standing is not cut to the new ceiling. See [[temple-demolition]].

### Cancelling builds and finding completed sites {#demolition-2}

Something still under construction is not demolished but cancelled, with its cost refunded: the ✕ in the Build queue, or `keryx cancel-build`.

`keryx build --list [city]` and Construct show the current level and the cost of the next level. Without a city name, Keryx uses your capital. Each hex building has its own level and upgrade price. A refusal names the building and the level it would reach.

Construction dispatches name the building, its city and the exact hex for a field building. **Staff Lumbermill** (or the named workplace) opens that city's Production grid with the completed site selected, so you can place a worker there. Buildings without a workplace offer **Show city** instead. The build queue repeats the city and field hex beside its completion time; Keryx shows the same place with `build --queue`.

## How the goods fit together

- **Food** is grain, fish and oil, eaten in proportion to what the city has ([[food]]). Wine is not food. Livestock is the emergency reserve.
- **Timber and stone** build nearly everything. Early on, timber is almost always your bottleneck.
- **Cedar stands in for timber:** whatever a cost needs in timber and you lack, your cedar covers one for one. Cedar also levels your best buildings and builds the [[war-galley|War Galley]].
- **Copper and tin** are the two halves of bronze, and they are never found together. Bronze arms the [[elite-infantry]], the [[war-chariot]], the War Galley and the best walls.
- **Silver** is the currency, and the only thing that pays professional soldiers and crews.
- **Incense** is rare, found only on marked dry hexes, and pleases [[gods|the gods]] more than any other offering.

## Economy tabs {#goods-the-three-tabs}

- **Goods** — stock, production and use of each good, city by city. The settlements table compares people, food produced minus food eaten, food game days and shortage status; select a city to close Economy and open its City drawer. Goods piling up with nothing using them are marked — see [[surplus]].
- **Transfer** — move goods between your own cities ([[transfers]]).
- **Routes & cargo** — [[routes|standing orders]] that move goods for you while you are away.

To learn what another city needs or can spare, ask its Wanax in a [[messengers|letter]] through **Diplomacy → Correspondence**, then agree a [[trade|trade offer]].

## Goods for offerings and trade {#goods-offerings-and-trade}

The gods weigh goods differently: bronze can count for far more than grain. **Kult**, at the temple, and `keryx rite --list` show their current reckoning before each god's preferences. What the world can spare and what the god favours both matter ([[rites]]). Wanaxes agree their own trade prices.

Production per game day is output before meals and other uses. Food net combines grain, fish and oil production minus population demand. The city has one stock of each good; food coverage counts these three goods together. Shortfall waiting estimates assume current production continues, before other use.

Food for people combines the three food goods minus the population’s meal. **Food after army** subtracts the food supplied by this city to its supported troops as well. The army shares grain, fish and oil in the same proportions; its silver pay is shown separately. Population growth still uses the population-only food balance.

## Storage capacity and forecasts {#goods-storage-capacity}

Each good has its own storage capacity in each city. A city stores **2 000 of each food** — grain, fish and oil — and a [[buildings|Granary]] raises that to 4 000, 10 000 and 20 000. The herd has its own pens. A city that already held more food when this ceiling came in keeps it and can eat it, but it never fills back above the ceiling. **StorageCapacityWarning** is an advance dispatch when the server forecasts a stock nearing its cap. Keryx status and the City drawer show the good, stored amount, capacity and **full in N game days**. The estimate uses the current net rate and deliveries on the way; it is a forecast, so changing production or orders can change it.

The forecast counts your own transports and accepted trade deliveries that you know about. An unsolicited gift from another Wanax is known only when it arrives, so it is not included beforehand.

Send goods away by [[transfers|transfer]] or use them in [[trade]]. Warehouse construction and storage-pool expansion are not available yet.

### Goods lost to full storage {#goods-storage-capacity-2}

A **StorageOverflow** notification means goods have already been lost because storage was full. It records the city, good, quantity lost and the source, such as production, a delivery, returned provisions or a refund. It does not mean the entire shipment was lost: only the reported excess failed to fit. Production into a store that stays full is lost every game day; you are told when it starts, not every game day it goes on. If the forecast clears and the city later approaches capacity again, a new warning can be sent.
silver:
**Silver is the currency and pays your professional forces.** [[elite-infantry]], [[war-chariot|chariots]] and [[war-galley|War Galleys]] need it; [[spearmen|spearmen]], [[galley|Galleys]] and [[emporos|Emporoi]] need no silver to recruit or maintain.

Professionals draw pay every game day. A Wanax who runs dry risks their desertion — see [[upkeep]].

## Where silver comes from

- **Out of the ground.** A silver deposit in your [[catchment]] and a **[[mine]]** built on that deposit hex ([[buildings]]) — the same building that works a [[copper|copper]] or [[tin|tin]] hex; the hex decides what it produces.
- **Out of someone else's ground, through [[trade]].** Most Wanaxes will not have a deposit. That is the point: silver is why the map has merchants on it.

Silver is kept with your other goods — the **Economy → Goods** tab shows your balance ([[goods]]).

Founding moves only the silver your Host still carries into the city: a new Host begins with **120 silver**, inland or coastal. Founding adds no extra silver. A Host rising after losing every city carries its remaining refugee purse. A [[colonies|colony]] carries existing silver from its mother city, rather than receiving new currency.
surplus:
Food storage is limited (see [[goods]] and [[granary]]); other goods can pile up to a million. Either way, **surplus is not free.**

The **Economy → Goods** tab marks goods that are piling up with nothing using them. The waste is not shelf space. It is the [[citizens]] standing on that hex, producing something nobody needs, when they could be growing food, cutting [[timber|timber]] or mining metal.

The fix is always the same: **move them.** Take them off the hex that overproduces and put them where the *next citizen would add* the most that you actually use. Or sell the surplus to someone who wants it ([[trade]] — ask a contacted Wanax what they need in a [[messengers|letter]]).

This is the most valuable habit in Megaron, and the one most players never build.
gifts:
A **gift or tribute** sends goods or [[silver|silver]] to another Wanax's city, with nothing requested in return. It needs no acceptance. The city must have a known location on your map, through sight, exploration or completed contact. A rumour alone is not enough.

Open **Economy → Transfer**. Choose your sending city, a destination marked with its Wanax's name **(gift)**, one or more goods and their quantities, then **Send →**. In Keryx, use `keryx transfer --good silver --qty 20 --dest CityName`; use the settlement ID if two cities share a name. Your own cities remain [[transfers|internal transfers]].

## Gifts in transit {#gifts-on-the-road}

The goods leave your stock when sent. They travel in a physical caravan, or aboard a real free ship from your port when a sea route is used. Cargo can be intercepted. A ship remains bound until its empty voyage home finishes. A gift carries the same risk as any other cargo: on land only raiders, at sea also [[sea|storms]].

A ship damaged in interception keeps the existing [[transfers|naval interception outcome]]: half of each good is lost, half sails home. The gift notice separates the exact quantities **lost** and **sent home**. This is a physical damaged return, not an immediate refund; that voyage can itself be intercepted.

## Receiving gifts {#gifts-at-the-destination}

The city receives only what fits in its store. Anything that does not fit is lost. **GiftDeliveredV2** or **GiftLostV2** tells you the exact quantities received and lost. There is no return of goods.

If the city changes hands during the journey, its **new owner receives the gift**. The sender, intended recipient and actual recipient are notified. If the city has fallen or has no owner, the gift is lost.

A gift appears as a row among the letters in **Diplomacy → Threads**. The sender can see its departure; the recipient sees the outcome when delivery is resolved. It creates no [[trade|trade offer]] and asks for nothing in return. Notifications and Keryx show the same delivery outcome.

To send goods between your own cities, use an [[transfers|internal transfer]].

The live cargo meter uses the same limits as an internal transfer: **[[galley]] 20 / [[emporos]] 120 goods**, one place per good of any kind. Several goods share one voyage.
transfers:
A **transfer** moves goods between two of your *own* settlements. No consent, no negotiation — simpler than [[trade]] with a stranger.

Open **Economy → Transfer**, choose *From*, *To*, the goods and their quantities, and press **Send →**. Below, **Your cargo in transit** lists everything on the road — which city it left, which city it is bound for, and its arrival time. A notification tells you when it is delivered.

## Physical cargo {#transfers-cargo-is-physical}

A caravan is people and pack animals walking across the map. Others can see it on the road, but not what it carries — the cargo is a secret until someone takes it. **It can be intercepted and seized** — yours by others, theirs by you. A hostile unit on watch ([[stances|sentry]]) near the road will stop a caravan that passes. Only [[messengers]] are safe. When a land caravan is seized, both sides are told where, and exactly what cargo changed hands; the seized goods go to the raider's capital.

An internal transfer carries exactly the same risk as a trade or a gift: on land only raiders, at sea also [[sea|storms]]. Whose goods they are never changes the risk.

To move goods regularly without being there, use a [[routes|standing order]].

## Naval transfer requirements {#transfers-sending-it-by-sea}

With automatic routing, when both ends are coastal or harboured and a sea lane connects them, a transfer sails instead of walking — **if you have a free [[galley]] or [[emporos]] waiting in the sending port** ([[sea]]). No free hull there, and no land road either, and the transfer is refused with the reason why; build one at a [[shipyard|Shipyard]], or wait for one to come home.

The ship is bound to the round trip: it cannot be given any other order until it has sailed back and unloaded, empty, at its own port. What it can carry is limited by the hull's own capacity — a shipment above the limit is refused before any goods leave your stock. **One good takes one cargo place**, whether [[grain|grain]], [[stone|stone]] or [[silver|silver]]: **Galley 20, Emporos 120 goods of any kind**. The form shows the ready hull and a live **Cargo used / capacity** meter; an overload tells you how much to remove. Land caravans have no cargo limit.

A laden ship caught at sea does not always lose the same way a caravan does. One of three things happens, and you are told which:

### Capture, damage and loss of cargo {#transfers-sending-it-by-sea-2}

- **Captured** — the raider takes the cargo *and* the ship. It sails off under a new flag.
- **Damaged** — half of every good is lost overboard in the fight; the ship limps home with the rest.
- **Sunk** — the cargo and the ship are both gone.

For a laden ship caught at sea:

| Outcome | Chance |
|---|---|
| Captured | 40% |
| Returns damaged | 40% |
| Sunk | 20% | <!-- src: server/internal/transport/intercept.go rollNavalSeizureOutcome -->

Sending to another Wanax is a [[gifts|gift or tribute]], with nothing requested in return.

## Cargo routes and travel time {#transfers-route-and-journey-time}

Cargo follows a real route around impassable ground. Its path and the [[terrain|terrain]] costs
are fixed when each leg departs. Caravan time is **1.5 times the march time on that
same path**, rounded once to the nearest whole game day, with at least one game day per leg.
The return leg is priced separately because it enters different terrain. Cargo
quantity limits a ship's hold; it does not change journey speed.

Without a traversable road or an eligible ship on a sea lane, a shipment is refused
before goods are taken. A standing route pauses and explains the obstacle. The
arrival time shown in your cargo list is the scheduled delivery; delays or
interception can prevent that delivery.

In Keryx, `transfer` sends from your **selected city**, which may be a [[colonies|colony]].
Check it with `keryx status`, or choose the sending city explicitly:
`keryx transfer --from Knossos --dest Mallia --good grain --qty 50`.
The sending city cannot also be the destination. A rejected self-transfer sends
nothing; use `--from` to choose the other city you meant to send from.

### Port approaches and mixed cargo {#transfers-route-and-journey-time-2}

A coastal city can load or receive through any adjacent navigable water hex. The sea route compares those approaches and chooses the fastest reachable one; it does not fix the port to an arbitrary side of the city. Journeys already at sea keep their saved route.

Choose several goods in the same form to send them together in **one shipment**:
one caravan or one ship, one arrival, one shared fate if intercepted or sunk.
Keryx accepts paired flags: `keryx transfer --dest Mallia --good grain --qty 12 --good timber --qty 8`.
Keryx shows the same cargo total and hull capacity before dispatch.

## Choosing land or sea {#transfers-choose-land-or-sea}

Economy → Transfer compares **Land** and **Sea** before you send a transfer or gift. Both show the journey in game days and real time, its arrival estimate, risk and requirements. An unavailable alternative explains why: a missing connected path, no departure/arrival coast or harbour, or no free ship with cargo space. Times assume departure now; an accepted agreement or standing route departs later and checks again. A preview reserves nothing.

Land cargo can be intercepted. Sea cargo can be intercepted and the ship can meet [[storms|storms]]; the same risks apply to your own goods, gifts, trade and standing routes. Sea needs your available Galley or Emporos at departure, enough cargo space and the existing voyage provisions.

Your selection is saved. An explicitly chosen land route never turns into a sea voyage, or vice versa, when conditions change. A standing route waits or pauses according to its existing rules if it cannot use the chosen mode. Older orders without a selection keep automatic routing.

### Land and sea choice in Keryx {#transfers-choose-land-or-sea-2}

Keryx: `transfer --by land --good grain --qty 50 --dest Petras`, or `--by sea`. The same flag works with `trade-offer` and `route`. Omit it for the existing automatic choice; the preview lists alternatives. For trade, the agreed choice covers the physical goods and payment legs, not the [[runners|runner]] carrying the offer.
routes:
A **standing order** is a land or sea cargo route that runs by itself. For a game that runs while you sleep, the **Economy → Routes & cargo** tab may be the most important screen you have.

Under **New standing order**, set *From*, *To*, and which end supplies the caravan's crew. Then:

## Standing route stock targets {#routes-details}

- **Keep at destination** — choose a good and the stock to keep there, for example two hundred [[grain|grain]] and fifty [[fish|fish]]. Use **Add a good** for another row and **Remove** to drop a row. The caravan keeps those goods topped up to that level at the destination.
- **Bring home** — choose a good and the stock to leave at the destination, for example twenty [[stone|stone]]. Zero means bring home everything available. Leave the rows empty for no return cargo. On the way back it brings home anything above that floor.

### Managing standing routes {#routes-details-2}

Press **Create route**. Existing routes are listed below with **Pause**, **Resume** and **Delete**. Each route shows **Keep at destination** (the target stock) and **Bring home above** (the stock left there before loading return cargo), including a zero floor. **Return cargo: none** means no goods are configured for the homeward leg. These are route settings; the cargo in each trip depends on available surplus and capacity. `keryx routes` shows the same settings. A route pauses itself when it cannot run — when there is no surplus to send, or no spare [[citizens|citizen]] to crew the caravan — and the list says why. You are told each time a route sends a caravan, and when it pauses.

## Uses for standing routes {#routes-what-to-use-it-for}

- Keeping a young [[colonies|colony]] fed until its own fields carry it.
- Supplying a city that has a mine but no farmland.
- Pulling [[timber|timber]] and stone to where you build.

Route caravans are [[transfers|cargo]] like any other, and can be raided on the road.

## Standing sea routes {#routes-sea-routes}

With automatic routing, a route between two coastal or harboured settlements with a sea lane between them sails instead of walking — if you have a free [[galley]] or [[emporos]] in the sending port ([[sea]]). That ship is then **locked to the route for as long as it runs**, including the time it spends docked between trips: it cannot be sent anywhere else, loaded, or repaired until the route is paused or deleted. No free hull, and no land road either, pauses the route with the same reason a shortfall would. The ship's hold limits both legs: out, it carries what fits; home, it brings back what fits above your floors, and the rest waits at the destination for the next trip.

Pause or delete a sea route and its ship comes free again: at once if it is sitting in port, empty-handed at the next sweep if it was sitting in the destination, or as soon as it finishes the leg it is already on.

## Standing route journey times {#routes-route-and-journey-time}

Cargo follows a real route around impassable ground. Its path and the [[terrain|terrain]] costs
are fixed when each leg departs. Caravan time is **1.5 times the march time on that
same path**, rounded once to the nearest whole game day, with at least one game day per leg.
The return leg is priced separately because it enters different terrain. The number
of goods limits a ship's hold; it does not change journey speed.

Without a traversable road or an eligible ship on a sea lane, a shipment is refused
before goods are taken. A standing route pauses and explains the obstacle. The
arrival game day shown in your cargo list is the scheduled delivery; delays or
interception can prevent that delivery.

## Following a route’s cargo {#routes-follow-your-cargo}

**Economy → Routes & cargo** shows the ship or caravan travelling on each
standing route, with its cargo and arrival. Other shipments are listed
separately. Both land and sea cargo live here; **War → Marches** is for the
forces you order to move. A route's ship remains in **War → Forces → Ships**,
with its route named on the card.

Choose **Land** or **Sea** in Routes & cargo before creating a route; Keryx uses `route --by land` or `route --by sea`. The choice is saved for subsequent departures. The comparison explains travel time, risk and unavailable alternatives; see [[transfers|land or sea]].
trade:
**A trade offer travels attached to a letter.** There is no market screen and no public listings. You write to a specific city and pin an offer to the message — so you can only trade with cities you have [[contact|contacted]]. A [[market|market board]] tells you what a city says it buys and sells, so you know whom to ask.

The **[[market]]** needs no workers. It has no staffing places; trade does not depend on assigning [[citizens|citizens]] to it.

## Making a trade offer {#trade-making-an-offer}

In a **Diplomacy → Correspondence** conversation (start one with **Known → Write**), expand **+ Attach trade offer** and choose:

- **Buy** — the good you want, the quantity, and the silver you offer. Your silver is held in escrow.
- **Sell** — the good you offer, the quantity, and the silver you want. Your goods are held in escrow.

Then **Dispatch →**. The offer walks with the [[messengers|messenger]], so it takes game days to arrive.

## Accepting or declining an offer {#trade-answering-an-offer}

A trade offer is a proposal whose goods or silver are held aside until it is answered or expires.

See [[trade-offer-expiry]] for the reply window.

An incoming offer appears in the conversation, for example *"Wants 40 [[tin|tin]] · Offers 200 silver"*, with **Accept ✓**, **Counter-offer** and **Decline ✗**. Your own pending offers carry **Cancel offer ✗** — withdraw it and your escrow comes back. If nobody answers before it expires, the escrow comes back too. Nothing is ever lost to silence.

The runner who carried your offer waits at the other city only while the offer is open: once it is accepted, declined or cancelled, the runner turns for home that same game day. **You learn the answer when the runner is home** — the news travels with the runner, never ahead of it. A declined offer's escrow travels with the runner too: your goods or silver are back in your stores the game day the runner is home. If the runner is lost at sea on the way, the escrow comes back at once. If nobody answers, no news comes: the offer lapses at its deadline, the escrow is back in your stores that same game day, and your letters show it as expired.

**Counter-offer.** If you like the trade but not the numbers, press **Counter-offer**. One line opens with the same good and the roles turned round — *Sell [40] tin for [200] silver* — and you change the numbers and press **Send**. Your own runner carries your terms back, and your goods or silver are held aside as in any offer. The other offer is declined in the same moment, and its runner goes home with its escrow. The other ruler must agree to your new terms; nothing is settled until they do. If your counter-offer cannot be sent (you lack the goods, or the offer has just expired), nothing changes and the original offer still stands.

## Delivering a trade agreement {#trade-delivery}

An accepted trade is carried along its agreed land or sea route. It arrives as a *Trade delivered* notification. On land nothing is lost by chance; like any [[transfers|cargo]] it can be raided. At sea every ship risks [[sea|storms]].

### When it goes by sea

With automatic routing, if both cities are coastal or harboured and a sea lane connects them, the trade sails instead of walking — carried by **your own** ship, whichever of you *sent* the offer. It makes the whole round trip: out with your half of the deal when the other side accepts, home again with their half. The other side's ships are never touched.

If you send an offer and have no free [[galley]] or [[emporos]] in your own port, and no land road connects the two cities either, the offer cannot be sent at all. If your only ship is taken by something else between sending and the other side's answer, their **Accept** fails and tells them so — your offer simply stays open until it expires or a ship frees up. A shipment too heavy for the ship's hold is refused the same way, naming the capacity.

### Returning damaged trade cargo {#trade-delivery-2}

The ship is not free for anything else until it is home — outbound and return both count, same [[transfers|three fates]] (captured, damaged, sunk) as any other cargo at sea. A **Damaged** outcome on the way home still gets half the cargo back to you, never to the other side.

## Finding trade partners {#trade-finding-partners}

Ask the Wanax of a [[contact|contacted]] city what they need or can spare. Write a [[messengers|letter]] in **Diplomacy → Correspondence** (start one with **Known → Write**), then negotiate in the reply before attaching a trade offer.

What is most worth trading? [[silver]], and the half of [[bronze]] you do not have.

## Trade agreement routes {#trade-route-and-journey-time}

Cargo follows a real route around impassable ground. Its path and the [[terrain|terrain]] costs
are fixed when each leg departs. Caravan time is **1.5 times the march time on that
same path**, rounded once to the nearest whole game day, with at least one game day per leg.
The return leg is priced separately because it enters different terrain. The number
of goods limits a ship's hold; it does not change journey speed.

Without a traversable road or an eligible ship on a sea lane, a shipment is refused
before goods are taken. A standing route pauses and explains the obstacle. The
arrival game day shown in your cargo list is the scheduled delivery; delays or
interception can prevent that delivery.

The seller receives the full agreed silver payment when it arrives. [[temple|Temples]] take no share of religious-goods sales.

Cargo follows its planned road or sea route one province at a time. The map and `keryx cargo` show its current province and arrival time. A province is reached only after its share of the full journey; the final province is reached at the announced arrival time.

### A trade agreement’s land or sea choice {#trade-route-and-journey-time-2}

Attach a trade offer in Letters and choose **Land** or **Sea** for the goods and payment. The runner still follows its own physical route. The choice stays with the agreement and is checked again on acceptance; Keryx uses `trade-offer --by land` or `--by sea`. See [[transfers|route requirements and risks]].

## Trade offer expiry {#trade-offer-expiry}

An offer’s expiry is the deadline for accepting or declining it.

New offers stay open for **24 game days after arrival**, and their runner waits for that same window. Offers already sent keep their recorded deadline. **Diplomacy → Letters** shows the reply deadline on your local clock; Keryx `outbox` shows when a pending offer expires.

No dispatch announces an expiry. At the deadline the offer lapses, its goods or silver are released back to your stores, and the letter reads *Expired without answer*.
