sight:
Sight determines which ground and moving people you can currently see.

You see the world at two depths: what you are looking at **now**, and what you **remember**.

## Live sight {#live-sight}

Every settlement, every unit standing on the map and every [[messengers|messenger]] on the road is an eye. A [[runners|Runner]] or messenger reveals the ground on the way out *and* on the way home.

| Eye | Sees |
|---|---|
| Settlement | 3 hexes |
| Land unit, or the [[horde|Nomadic Host]] | 2 hexes |
| Ship | 1 hex of land — a ship is blind inland, but sees the shoreline across the water it sees |
| Anyone, looking at a mountain | 2 hexes further — mountains are landmarks |
| Anyone standing at open water | 4 hexes of sea — in a straight line across open water only |
<!-- src: server/internal/province/hex.go LiveRadius, SeaSightline -->

### Seeing shorelines from ships {#live-sight-2}

The open horizon belongs to whoever stands at the water, and it reaches only across open water in a straight line. A coastal city or a ship reads the sea out to four hexes, but only where nothing but sea lies between it and the hex it looks at: an island, a headland or a strip of shore in the way blocks the view beyond it. An army on the beach does not see a lake behind it over the [[hills|hills]], and an army two hexes inland does not see the sea at all beyond its ordinary two hexes. A [[rivers|river]] between banks is not the sea and opens no horizon. **A ship also sees the shore:** every coast hex that borders water on its horizon shows, so sailing along a coast maps the coastline — but not the land behind it. <!-- src: server/internal/province/hex.go SetSeaHorizons -->

## Map memory {#map-memory}

The map shows **colour for live sight, grayscale for remembered ground, and black for places never seen**. Remembered ground keeps its [[terrain|terrain]] details, frozen as you last saw it. It can be wrong, and it will not tell you so.

**A city on remembered ground is shown as you last saw it**: its name, its ruler, its walls and its size, with the time you saw it. If it has changed hands or burned since then, you will not know until someone sees it again. A city founded on ground you saw while it was empty does not appear in your memory, because you remember the empty ground. A [[messengers|messenger]] that reaches a city also lets you see it at that moment. <!-- src: server/internal/province/seen_settlements.go RecordSeenSettlements -->

**Foreign forces are drawn only on ground you can see live**, never on remembered ground. They are drawn with a blinking outline.

## Moving actors on the map {#map-actors}

Your marching armies, ships, Runners and [[transfers|caravans]] always show their **remaining route ahead**, beginning where the actor is now. The line shrinks as they travel; nothing is drawn behind them. Solid lines mark armies, long dashes mark ships, dots mark Runners, and mixed long/short dashes mark caravans. The line shows only ground you can see live.

A foreign actor shows only a **compass arrow at its current live position**. It tells you which way the actor goes now, never its destination or full route. Your lines are azure; foreign arrows use the foreign unit's muted accent. Line patterns and arrow shapes carry meaning alongside colour. An agreed trade caravan coming to you shows its remaining route too, in the foreign accent. Its known cargo and arrival remain in the trade details. Gifts are not agreed deliveries and show only an arrow. A Runner coming to you from another Wanax also shows only an arrow. Waiting or sealed Runners have no forward route, and a Runner aboard follows the real carrier. Runners remain sacred and cannot be attacked.
sea:
Ships carry people, messages and goods across navigable water.

The sea is **the Thalassa**. It carries your ships, your traders and your ambitions — and it is how you reach the half of [[bronze]] your own land does not have.

## Sea storms and ship damage {#sea-storm-risks}

The open sea is never quite safe, but **you can see its storms** — see [[storms]]. A storm is three sea hexes of dark cloud that drift slowly across the Thalassa; a ship that crosses any of them takes the damage, even between the game day's start and end, whatever the ship is doing — a fleet, a ship carrying an army, an expedition, a [[galley|galley]] carrying a trade, a [[transfers|transfer]] or a gift. A storm can also drift onto a slow ship. Whose ship it is and why it sails never change that. Rivers and land have no storms. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/sea_storm_weather.go SeaHexesPerStorm -->

### Damage from entering a storm {#sea-storm-risks-2}

- **Each storm costs the ship two points of hull** (of five), once, however many game days it spends inside that storm. Three storms sink a ship that began with full hull. You are told where it struck and how much hull is left.
- **At hull 0 the ship founders.** It goes down with everything aboard: its crew, any troops it carries, and any cargo. You are told where, and what was lost with her.
- A battered ship keeps sailing. Bring it home and **Repair** it at a [[shipyard|Shipyard]] before its next long voyage.
naming-the-land:
The first Wanax whose **own physical unit reaches** a [[rivers|river]], mountain massif, [[semi-desert|desert]] or [[cedar-forest|cedar forest]] gains the right to name it. Seeing the place nearby gives no right. You receive a notice naming the unit that reached it first.

For a river, desert or cedar forest, your unit must enter one of its hexes. For a mountain massif, your unit must enter **land directly bordering the mountains**. Mountains remain impassable. If that land borders two separate massifs, you gain the right to name both. Simply seeing mountains from farther away gives no naming right.

## Naming known land {#naming-the-land-details}

A river includes its [[river-ford|fords]] and connected [[river-delta|delta]]. A mountain massif joins neighbouring limestone and [[red-mountains|red mountains]]; a desert joins neighbouring desert hexes; a cedar forest joins neighbouring [[cedar|cedar]] woodland. Massifs, deserts and cedar forests must cover at least five hexes to be named. Olive groves are cultivated land and cannot be named this way.

## Giving a place a name {#naming-the-land-give-it-a-name}

Click any known hex of the place on the map. If the right is yours, its panel offers a name box. The right lasts until used, with no time limit. **You may name it once.** A nameless place keeps its [[terrain|terrain]] title and has no name label on the map.

Names are trimmed, 2–30 characters, and may contain letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes and hyphens. A name must be unique in the world, ignoring letter case. Naming is immediate: it sends no order or [[runners|Runner]].

After naming, the name appears in the hexpanel and on the map at readable zoom. The TERRAIN row still describes the ground. Only hexes you can see or remember reveal the place and its name; naming never reveals unknown land. See [[sight]].

## Naming places in Keryx {#naming-the-land-keryx}

`keryx places` lists known places, their kind and anchor id (`q,r`), their known hexes, and whether you may name them.

`keryx places name river 6,79 "Alpheios"` names a river. Use `massif`, `desert` or `forest` for the other kinds, with the id shown in your list. Add `--json` for the complete API reply. If an anchor starts with a minus sign, put `--` before the positional arguments: `keryx places name -- river -6,79 "Alpheios"`.

Administrators can change or remove unsuitable names with `keryx places rename <kind> <q,r> "<name>"` or `keryx places unname <kind> <q,r>` and their admin key. Removing a name leaves the naming right spent.

Once a place has a name, anyone who has seen it can tell others of it in a letter. See [[telling-of-places]].

Storms follow their own rule: the first ship struck by a storm earns its naming right. See [[storms]].
storms:
A **storm** is three connected hexes of dark cloud on the Thalassa. There is about one for every 100 hexes of sea, and they never stop wandering. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/sea_storm_weather.go SeaHexesPerStorm -->


Select a water hex on the world map or in the city's workforce grid to read any known storm there. An open panel follows incoming weather updates; workers stay placed while a storm stops fishing. Keryx `storms` lists known storm coordinates, and `status` reports affected fishing grounds.

## How storms move {#storms-how-they-move}

Each game day a storm takes **two steps**. In each step, one of its three hexes moves to a neighbouring sea hex, and the storm stays in one piece. So a storm crawls: slowly, and a little more each game day in the direction it has been drifting, now and then turning. It never crosses land.

## Storm effects {#storms-what-they-do}

A ship that **sails into a storm** takes two points of hull damage (of five) — once per storm, however many game days it spends inside it; three storms sink a ship from full hull. At hull 0 she founders with everything aboard ([[sea]]). A ship beside a storm is safe. Ships follow the route they were given and cannot steer round a storm once they sail ([[sea]]), so look before you send them.

Every sea hex a ship crosses is checked, even when it crosses several in one game day. Two different storms crossed that game day each strike; staying inside the same storm gives no extra blow. A storm can also drift onto a slow ship. [[rites|Favourable Passage]] still protects the ship on its outward leg.

A storm standing on a city's fishing hex stops the fishing there until it moves on ([[fishing]]).

## Seeing and remembering storms {#storms-what-you-see}

You see a storm **only inside your own sight** ([[sight]]) — from your cities, your ships and your soldiers. There it is drawn as dark cloud, and hovering tells you which way it is drifting.

Once you have seen a storm, the map remembers it **where you last saw it**, as a faded cloud, and hovering says on which game day. That is not where it is now. If you see any part of that place and the storm is not there, it has moved on and the memory is dropped.

## Naming a storm {#storms-naming-a-storm}

The first Wanax whose ship a storm strikes **may [[naming-the-land|name it]]**, once — even if that blow sinks the ship. You are told in the storm notice. Click the storm on the map and give it a name (2 to 30 letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes and hyphens; no two storms share a name). The storm keeps the name wherever it drifts, and everyone who sees or remembers it will see the name. A name that is out of order can be changed or removed by the game's keepers; the one who gave it does not get a second try.

In Keryx: `storms` lists the storms in sight and the ones you remember, with their ids; `storms name <id> "<name>"` names one you were first to meet.

**Fishers stay at their grounds.** A storm makes them catch nothing while it covers their hex; it never sends them home or removes their placement. They resume fishing when it moves on. See [[fishing]].
units:
Forces are the soldiers, ships and people you command.

The **War (⚔)** drawer has three tabs: **Forces**, **Recruit** and **Marches**.

## Recruitment costs and requirements {#units-recruiting}

**War → Recruit.** Choose the city at the top if you hold several. Each row shows the total cost of one order and how many men or crew it drafts from the city. An unavailable row keeps that price visible and names what is missing, including the required amount and what the city has.

| Force | Needs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **[[spearmen|Spearman]]** | [[barracks]] | The levy. 12 [[grain|grain]] for one 100-man cohort; no silver. |
| **[[elite-infantry|Bronze Guard]]** | Barracks + [[foundry]] | Costs [[bronze]]. Far harder per man. |
| **[[war-chariot|Chariot]]** | [[stable]] | Costs bronze. The hardest hitter on the field. |
| **[[galley|Galley]]** | [[shipyard|Shipyard]] | 30 [[timber|timber]] (or [[cedar|cedar]]); no silver. Transport and sight at sea ([[sea]]). |
| **[[war-galley|War Galley]]** | Shipyard + Foundry | Costs cedar. The warship. |
| **[[emporos|Emporos]]** | Shipyard | 90 cedar; no timber or silver. Trade hull; carries the most goods and up to three land forces, no warship. |

Timber costs can be paid with cedar, one for one. Timber is used first; cedar fills the shortfall. Cedar specifically required by an order must still be available before any spare cedar can cover timber.

### Cohort training and readiness {#units-recruiting-2}

Land forces train as a whole hundred-man cohort (**Train 100**). Ships are built one at a time and can be named. Their cost and population draft cover the ship's crew, rather than a hundred-man cohort. Rowers eat like spearmen: the actual surviving crew draws a port ration at home and double on a mission ([[upkeep]]). Rejected recruitment consumes no people or goods. The completion dispatch names the ready unit type and its city — for example, “Emporos ready in Tylissos”. **Show the ship** or **Review the unit** opens its highlighted Forces card. If the unit no longer exists, the dispatch does not offer an empty unit view. A cohort still gathering men or training cannot march. Once ready, it can still march after losing men; it does not have to refill to 100 first.

Every cohort is numbered by its home city: **2nd Spearmen of Knossos**. A lost regiment's number is never given out again. Before you found your first city, your [[horde]]'s two escort cohorts carry your own name instead — **1st** and **2nd Spearmen of** *you* — and become the new city's 1st and 2nd when you settle.

## Drafting and supporting forces {#units-recruits-are-your-own-people}

A cohort is drafted out of your city's population and stays out of it until disbanded. Soldiers still eat. **Spearmen, Galleys and Emporoi draw 0 silver per game day**. Bronze Guard, chariots and War Galleys draw pay in [[silver]]. Home service costs half field pay: a full elite cohort draws 0.75 / 1.5 silver per game day at home / in the field, and a full chariot cohort 2 / 4. A full War Galley draws 0.25 / 0.5 ([[upkeep]]). An army bigger than your city can feed and pay is not a strong army; it is a famine with spears.

In each combat round, **100 active spearmen roll 50 dice**. Half the active men roll, rounded up: one man rolls one die, three roll two. Bronze Guard rolls three dice per active man and chariots five per chariot. A **War Galley rolls 5 dice**, against a **Galley's 1** before hull damage and other [[battle|battle]] adjustments.

### Disbanding and supporting city stores {#units-recruits-are-your-own-people-2}

**Disband** selects a whole unit by name in City → Garrison. Its remaining people return to that city: a full Spearmen cohort returns 100 people; a damaged cohort returns only its survivors. There is no soldier-quantity input. Ships return their actual crew; a laid-up hull returns no crew a second time. Keryx: `disband --unit "<unit name>"` or `disband --unit <unit-id> --province <city>`; repeat `--unit` to select several whole forces in that city. The receipt names each unit before its returned people and city: “2nd Spearmen of Phaistos disbanded — 41 people return to Phaistos.” Selecting several forces gives one sentence per unit. Silver is unchanged.

### Laying up and fitting out crews {#units-recruits-are-your-own-people-3}

An empty ship in your own active [[harbour|Harbour]] can be **Laid up** from its Forces card. Its crew returns to the port's population and can work there; the hull draws no food or silver and remains in port. The card says **Laid up** and offers **Fit out**. Fitting out takes the ship's full crew from that city's current population and prepares it for **three game days**. It cannot sail or be cancelled during that time, and its crew draws home-rate food and, for a War Galley, half field pay from the start. If the city is annexed, its laid-up and fitting-out ships go with the city. Disbanding a laid-up ship removes the hull without returning the same crew twice; choose the particular hull to disband by its name. Keryx: `unit lay-up --unit ID` and `unit fit-out --unit ID`.

## Reading the Forces roster {#units-the-forces-tab}

Every unit you own, with its state and current grain and silver upkeep per game day in plain words. **March** is shown while it can move; a damaged land cohort garrisoned in its **original home city** can also **Reinforce** — another city you own does not qualify. Reinforcing adds at most **4 men per game day**, taken only from that game day's population growth, so the city never shrinks to refill a cohort. A land unit on the march shows **Recall**. The card also shows stance and **Set**, battle retreat, **Redirect**, **Fetch by ship**, **Load** / **Unload** or **Repair**, whenever that unit can use them. Choose **Destination city** in a march or redirect form to target a known city quickly; map clicks remain available. Keryx accepts `--to "City name"` on march, post and redirect. See [[marching]], [[stances]] and [[sea]].

**Marches** lists your forces on the march (**Your Marches**) and every foreign unit you can see marching on one of your settlements (**Incoming**), soonest arrival first. You only see an incoming column once one of your eyes has it in sight — the *foreign march sighted* notification fires at the same moment ([[defence]]).

**Forces on a hex:** select their current hex on the map to inspect the same force cards, your own first. A marching force appears where it is now. Ships show hull, passengers and available provision information; orders and their destination remain visible. A pending [[messengers|messenger]] is still carrying an order, which takes effect when delivered. **View in Forces** opens the selected force. **Redirect** selects that force and asks for a new destination; **Recall** sends its existing return order. Ships on missions at sea take neither command. On a narrow screen, expand a force's row for details. Your own cities continue to open the City drawer.

`keryx hex <q,r>` lists the forces at that coordinate and the corresponding commands. A foreign force shows only observed information: owner, kind, strength, status, heading and any reported passengers. Its hull, provisions, orders and actual destination are unknown; a movement that *seems* bound for one of your cities remains an estimate. See [[map-actors]].

### Cancelling training and cargo capacity {#units-the-forces-tab-2}

Recruitment confirms that your order was received. While a unit is still training, use **Cancel training** in War → Forces to return its people and reserved resources. A ship under construction has **Cancel build**. In Keryx use `unit cancel-training --unit ID`. Finished forces use Disband instead.

For goods, a **Galley carries 20** and an **Emporos carries 120 goods of any kind**. One good takes one cargo place; several goods can share a single [[transfers|shipment]]. A ship carrying a land unit is unavailable for goods freight.

## Forces, Marches and commerce {#units-forces-and-marches}

**Forces** groups your roster as **Land Forces**, **Ships** and, only while you
have a Nomadic Host, **People**. Being in harbour, marching, aboard another
ship or laid up is shown on each card. A ship bound to a standing route stays
under Ships and names its route, including between legs.

**Marches** lists your ordered marches, sailings, landings, expeditions and
returns, together with known incoming threats. Automated trade is under
**Economy → Routes & cargo**, where each standing route shows its travelling
ship or caravan. Other shipments, including agreements, transfers and gifts,
have their own cargo list there. See [[routes]] and [[transfers]].

`keryx forces` shows the same roster. Older `units`, `army` and `unit list`
commands remain accepted.

## War Galley combat power {#war-galley-why-it-is-dangerous}

A War Galley is not a thicker or better-armoured ship. It is dangerous because of who is aboard: rowers, archers, slingers and boarding fighters — a trained marine force, not ordinary oarsmen or soldiers carried as passengers. In a sea fight it shoots at the enemy from a distance, then closes to board or force a surrender. That is why it rolls 5 dice where a Galley or an Emporos rolls 1.

It is also why only the War Galley costs silver and draws pay. A Galley or an Emporos is rowed by ordinary men from the city; a War Galley keeps standing marines.

So it is a costly specialist. It strikes hard and is the fastest ship at sea, but it has the same 5 hull points as any other hull. Three Galleys roll fewer dice together, yet carry three times the hull — a real danger to it, more so once it is damaged.

Build it when ships must fight or hunt other ships. It carries no cargo, so trade stays with the [[galley]] and the [[emporos]]. See [[units|Forces]] and [[battle]].

marching:
**Right-click a destination**, select your forces and check the forecast before sending. Use **Explore** for unknown ground. Orders to forces in the field travel by Runner; ships must receive their whole mission in port ([[ship-types]]).

## Selecting forces for a march {#marching-giving-a-march-order}

**Right-click the destination hex.** The order menu shows what the destination is, which of your forces can go and **March →**. Only one unit is selected initially. Select the checkbox beside each named unit you want to order; forces sharing a type or location are separate choices. **More** holds stance ([[stances]]), expedition duration and column name.

You can also left-click a hex and use **March here →** — or **Send [[galley|galleys]] →** at sea, or **Colonize →** on empty land ([[colonies]]). Hovering those buttons previews the result on the map.

Choose the named forces to send and the menu estimates each selected unit’s arrival **before you send the order**. **War → Forces → March** selects that unit; click a destination on the map to open the same menu. Ships with different crews or cargo may arrive at different times. The estimate uses the current route and speed; conditions can change before arrival.

### March forecasts and city destinations {#marching-giving-a-march-order-2}

If a [[messengers|messenger]] must first deliver the order, or the destination is unexplored, the forecast says why arrival is not yet known. Redirects also wait for a messenger; their current course continues until delivery. The **Sold** line shows the selected forces’ [[silver|silver]] drain at home and in the field, and how long their paying city’s treasury lasts after departure; with several paying cities, it shows the shortest treasury duration; [[spearmen|spearmen]] show **0 → 0**. No forecast sends an order.

In Keryx, use `march --unit <id> --target q,r --preview` (or `unit march` with the same flags). Add `--json` for the server forecast. Omit `--preview` when you are ready to send. `--unit` also accepts an exact unit name, for example `--unit "3rd Spearmen of Tylissos"`; names are case-insensitive and an ambiguous name is refused.

**Choose a city quickly:** the order menu's **Destination city** list offers your own cities first, followed by cities you have actually seen, remembered or contacted. Selecting one fills the destination; you can still choose a hex on the map. A city known only through rumours is not a destination yet. The confirmation names the city.

### City destinations in Keryx {#marching-giving-a-march-order-3}

In Keryx, `march --unit <id> --to "Pylos"` chooses that city's exact hex. The same shortcut works for `unit march`, `unit post` and `unit redirect`, including march previews. Use `--to`, `--target q,r` or `--q/--r`, one form at a time. If two known cities share a name, Keryx lists the candidates and asks for coordinates. An unknown city name is refused. Selecting a city does not change which missions are valid there: a patrol still needs [[coastal-sea|coastal water]], so patrol has no city shortcut.

A notification tells you when a unit arrives.

## Redirecting a moving force {#marching-a-marching-unit-is-still-reachable}

Right-click a new destination and a unit already marching shows up in the menu too, marked **on the march → redirect by messenger**. Pick it like any other unit — the order is a **Redirect**, not a fresh march: the unit keeps going on its old course until the Runner reaches it, then turns onto the new one. You can also redirect from the unit’s **War → Forces** row, including by typed coordinates.

## Recall and Redirect by Runner {#marching-orders-to-forces-already-in-the-field-travel-by-runner}

A unit standing in its city hears you at once. A unit out in the field does not — **Recall** and **Redirect** are carried by a [[runners|Runner]], and the game estimates his next meeting with the unit. The horn sounds when the soldiers *receive* the order, not when you give it.

Recall turns an expedition home to its city, where it rejoins the garrison and files its report ([[sight]]). An ordinary march returns to its departure hex. Redirect sends the unit to the destination you choose.

**War → Forces → Recall all**, or `keryx recall --all`, sends a separate recall order to each of your marching forces.

### Recalling all and keeping failed orders {#marching-orders-to-forces-already-in-the-field-travel-by-runner-2}

Recall and redirect need a passable route from the unit’s current position. If its position or the new route cannot be resolved, the order is refused with a reason. If the Runner cannot catch up during the march, it goes to the destination. For a newly sent land order, if the unit has moved again, the Runner keeps the same order and takes a new physical route to catch it. The order takes effect only when they meet. While the Runner follows a moving unit, **War → Forces** and `keryx unit list` show the next meeting estimate, which can change; it is not a guaranteed delivery time. If the Runner must wait before continuing, they show that instead of a delivery time. A destroyed unit or a unit you no longer own cannot receive the order. A Runner-delivered refusal appears in Dispatches; the unit keeps its existing course. Check the unit and choose a reachable destination.

## Passable destinations {#marching-where-you-can-march}

- **A plain march only reaches ground your people have already seen.** Right-click an unseen hex and the order menu offers **Explore** instead — the unit explores the surrounding area and returns home with a report ([[sight]]).
- Crossing the sea needs ships ([[sea]]).
- A march that cannot go on — its path blocked, or impossible — stalls, and you are told why.

## Forces travelling on a route {#marching-on-the-road}

The unit moves hex by hex once it receives its order. The map and `keryx unit list` show its reached hex and estimated arrival. Sight opens along the way; [[storms]] and enemies can interrupt the journey.

A marching army eats more than one in garrison and cannot forage ([[upkeep]]). It is seen by anyone whose [[sight]] it passes through, and an enemy on watch may stop it — and a [[battle]] begins by itself. **There is no declaration of war.**

## Ordering an expedition {#marching-exploring-an-area}

Choose **Explore** in the map menu; the default expedition duration is ready to use. Open **More** to change the duration in **game days**. The chosen hex is the centre of an area, even in fog. The order summary shows its extent and duration before sending; **War → Forces → March** offers the same controls.

It travels first to the exact hex you chose, even if that hex is already seen, then chooses nearby unexplored ground on its own. It turns home by half the duration. It can turn earlier if the area is already explored or nothing further is reachable. **War → Forces** and `keryx unit list` show the area, duration, latest turn and home game day, and why it has turned. A Runner-delivered order begins when received, so those game days become known when it starts. On return, Dispatches carries the report ([[sight]]).

### Expedition destinations and duration {#marching-exploring-an-area-2}

The chosen hex is the first destination. If it cannot be reached from this unit's position, the order is refused without substituting another destination. Choose a reachable hex or use a unit departing from elsewhere. After reaching the chosen hex, a ship prefers unseen coastal water over open sea.

In Keryx: `unit march --unit <id> --target q,r --intent explore --ticks N`. Omit `--ticks` for the server's default duration; the current allowed range comes from the game. Add `--preview` to check the order without dispatching. Exploration routes cross unknown ground, so their arrival forecast stays unavailable.

## Land terrain and travel time {#marching-terrain-and-journey-time}

For foot soldiers, each plain, [[river-valley|river valley]] or [[river-delta|delta]] takes **1 game day**; [[olive-grove|olive groves]]
and [[maquis|maquis]] **1.5 game days**; [[hills|hills]] and [[cedar-forest|cedar forest]] **2 game days**; [[semi-desert|semi-desert]] **3 game days**.
A [[river-ford|ford]] takes **2.5 game days** on foot. Mountains cannot be crossed.
[[war-chariot|Chariots]] are fast on the flat and slow everywhere else: **0.67 game days** on a
plain, river valley or delta, **2 game days** in olive groves and maquis, and
**3 game days** in hills, cedar forest and semi-desert. A ford takes them 2.5 game days
too. The [[horde|Nomadic Host]]
needs twice the foot soldiers' time. A Runner takes half the foot time on land.

### Ship speed and expedition forecasts {#marching-terrain-and-journey-time-2}

A fully crewed Galley sails **3 coastal hexes per game day** or **5 deep-sea hexes per
game day**, **2 [[rivers|river]] hexes per game day**, and takes **1 game day** through a ford — with the current it takes half the time, against it twice ([[rivers]]). A [[war-galley]]
needs 60% of the Galley's time; an [[emporos]] needs 140%. A short crew or a carried
land unit slows a marching ship. Runners aboard follow their carrier's journey.
Cargo journeys use the separate [[routes|caravan rule]]: 1.5 times the base route
time, including at sea; cargo does not change their speed.

These are base costs before rounding the whole journey to at least one game day.
Travel time is fixed at departure; later rule changes do not recalculate a journey already underway. A finished
[[roads|road]] shortens the hex it leads into for everyone who walks it.

An expedition preview shows its planned length. For a unit in garrison it can also show the planned homecoming **if it departed immediately**. The order may still need physical delivery. The preview names the selected first destination; its route and arrival time remain undisclosed.

### Expedition budget and superseded orders {#marching-terrain-and-journey-time-3}

A march preview applies the same expedition budget checks as the order. Before sending an expedition, both the web menu and Keryx check its duration without dispatching anything. A refused or unavailable validation sends no Runner: choose a longer duration or a nearer area. A valid expedition may still have an unavailable arrival time. Unseen routes and their travel times remain undisclosed. A Host founds with `founding settle`, not a colony march. Without confirmation, nothing is sent.

If you send a new movement order to the same unit while an earlier order Runner still waits unboarded in one of your ports, the earlier order is withdrawn in the same dispatch. That Runner walks home; the new order still travels physically. A Runner already aboard a ship or travelling elsewhere continues on its own course, and an independent stance order is unaffected. Your dispatch receipt says when it withdrew an earlier order.
roads:
A road is a built connection between neighbouring land hexes.

<!-- src: server/internal/combat/road.go, server/internal/province/roads.go -->
A **road** is a worn way between two neighbouring hexes, built by an army out of [[stone|stone]]. Once it stands, **everyone** who walks it travels faster — your people, your [[messengers|messengers]], your caravans, and your enemy's. It never decays and needs no [[upkeep|upkeep]].

## Road movement costs {#roads-what-a-road-does}

On a road, every hex you **enter** takes the same time **whatever the ground** — a hill or [[semi-desert|desert]] hex costs no more than a plain. Time per hex over a road edge:

| Traveller | Time per hex on a road |
|---|---|
| Foot soldiers | 0.75 game day |
| Runners and messengers | 0.35 game day |
| Caravans | 0.6 game day |
| [[war-chariot|Chariots]] | 0.4 game day |
| Ships | no effect |

(Off the road a foot soldier needs 1 game day on [[plains|plains]], 2 on [[hills|hills]] and 3 in semi-desert, so a road helps most where the ground is hardest.)

Roads join **land** hexes: plains, [[river-valley|river valley]], [[river-delta|river delta]], [[olive-grove|olive groves]], [[maquis|maquis]], hills, [[cedar-forest|cedar forest]] and semi-desert. They never cross water or mountains, and there are **no bridges** — a road ends at a [[rivers|river]] [[river-ford|ford]] and the ford is waded as before.

## Building a road {#roads-building-one}

**War → Forces → Build road** (or `keryx unit build-road --unit <id> --to q,r`) orders one army to build **one edge**, from the hex it stands on to a neighbouring hex. For a longer road, give another order.

The **stone** leaves your nearest city the moment you give the order — you are told at once if it has too little. It travels as a caravan to the first hex, and a [[runners|Runner]] carries the order to the army, which marches there. **Building starts only when both the stone and the army are at the first hex.**

| Ground the road reaches | Stone |
|---|---|
| Plains, river valley, delta | 8 |
| Olive grove, maquis | 12 |
| Hills, cedar forest | 16 |
| Semi-desert | 24 |

Three plains edges cost 24 stone. A hundred men build a plains edge in **1 game day** and a hill edge in **2**; fewer men take longer. When the edge is finished you get a **RoadEdgeBuilt** notice.

## Interrupted road construction {#roads-when-it-goes-wrong}

- The stone caravan is a physical caravan and **can be intercepted** ([[transfers]]). Then the road is not finished and the stone is lost.
- A **new order** to the army cancels its unfinished road. The army being destroyed or drawn into a [[battle]] before the edge is done ends it too. **Stone is never refunded.**
- A road still waiting for its stone or its army stays listed — `keryx roads` shows what each is waiting for.

## Seeing roads {#roads-seeing-roads}

You see a road edge only where your people have seen or remember **both** of its hexes. Unfinished roads of your own are drawn dotted.

Related: [[marching]], [[transfers]].
defence:
In a game where nobody is online all the time, defence is mostly a matter of **knowing early** — and then having time to answer.

## Incoming march warnings {#defence-you-are-told-when-something-comes}

When a foreign army is seen marching, you get a *foreign march sighted* notification. It only fires if one of your eyes sees it: a settlement, a unit, a [[messengers|messenger]] on the road ([[sight]]).

You see **which way it is going — never where**. An army walking round a mountain can look, for a while, as if it were heading somewhere else. If its heading points at the lands of one of your cities, the notice says so and tells you **when it would get there, if that is its goal**. Treat that as a warning, not a promise: it may turn. If it turns toward you later, you are warned again.

## Physical warning time {#defence-why-the-defender-has-time}

Orders are physical ([[runners]]). The attacker's army walks the whole distance to you; your answer usually has a much shorter way to go — from your city to the nearby forces, or to the garrison already there. **Distance is the defender's ally.**

## Buying time to defend {#defence-buying-warning-time}

- Post forces in **sentry** on the approaches — roads, [[rivers|river]] crossings, the coast ([[stances]]).
- Keep a ship at sea near your coast.
- Well-filled [[food|food stores]] buys time against a [[sieges|siege]].
- [[walls|Walls]] absorb damage in [[battle]] ([[buildings]]).

When you come back after being away, **foreign marches are among the first things to read** ([[coming-back]]).
battle:
**There is no declaration of war.** If your army arrives where a hostile army is, or a unit on watch catches a march going by, a battle starts by itself.

## When battle begins {#battle-when-battle-begins}

If your forces or city come under attack, a dispatch names the opponent and place. Choose **Take me there** to see it. Muted dispatches remain in **Notifications**.

## Battle rounds {#battle-how-a-battle-runs}

**A battle can last several game days.** Each game day the two sides clash three times. In every clash, 90% of each side's men take part and roll twelve-sided dice. **A 12 is a hit**, and every hit costs the enemy one man, one chariot, or a blow to a ship's hull. Losses are shared among a side's forces in proportion to their size.

| | Dice in each clash |
|---|---|
| [[spearmen|Spearmen]] | 1 for every 2 men |
| [[elite-infantry|Bronze Guard]] | 3 per man |
| [[war-chariot|Chariot]] | 5 per chariot |
| [[war-galley|War Galley]] | 5 per ship |
| [[galley|Galley]], [[emporos|Emporos]] | 1 per ship |

So 100 spearmen put 90 men in a clash, roll 45 dice and can expect about 4 hits; 100 Bronze Guard roll 270 dice and can expect about 22. This is what [[bronze]] buys. A damaged ship rolls fewer dice, in proportion to its remaining hull.

**[[walls|Walls]].** Each game day the wall takes the first **20 hits per wall level** aimed at the defenders before any of them falls. An attacker in the **storm** stance halves what the wall stops, but every hit the defenders land on the stormers counts **one and a half times** ([[stances]]).

**Breaking.** A side that has lost enough routs and withdraws with its survivors; annihilation is the exception. You choose how much is "enough" for your whole realm under **War → Forces → When to retreat**: **Hold to the last man** or **Retreat when it goes badly** (the default, retreating when 20% of starting strength remains). You can override it for one unit in the battle it is fighting; see [[stances]]. If both sides break on the same game day, both withdraw and nobody wins.

**Reinforcements** that reach a battle already under way join it.

## Battle reports and survivors {#battle-after-the-battle}

You are told the outcome, with the losses on both sides — for example *"Victory at Petras — your [[spearmen|spearmen]] (100→61) vs Idomeneus's chariots (40→12). The field was taken."* You hear the clash of arms if sound is on.

**Ships after a battle.** Every surviving ship of a side loses hull in proportion to that side's losses; soldiers aboard lose the same share of their men. A ship whose hull reaches 0 sinks with everyone on board. Repair it at a [[shipyard|Shipyard]] ([[ship-types|Ships]]). <!-- src: server/internal/combat/ship_hull.go -->

Winning at a city does not make it yours. It becomes **occupied** — see [[occupation]]. A city can also be taken without any battle at all, by [[food|hunger]]: see [[sieges]].

**[[mistress-of-the-walls]]** ([[rites]]) strengthens only the casting Wanax's own garrison defending the blessed city, for 6 game days. It gives no bonus to an attacker, a field army or a new owner of the city.
occupation:
Winning at a city — by [[battle]] or by [[sieges|siege]] — does not make it yours. It becomes **occupied**: still owned by its Wanax, garrisoned by the victor's survivors, its production frozen.

**Hold it for 30 game days without a fight and you may annex it.** **Any new fighting at the city starts the count again.** The defender can send a relief force.

## Completing an occupation {#occupation-when-the-occupation-ripens}

You do not have to wait for the full count. As soon as the city falls you may:

- **sack** it. Your men carry off half its [[silver|silver]] and a share of its other goods (you may choose which), its best production building loses a level, and a third of its people are lost (it never falls below 50). The city stays theirs. The loot goes home as a caravan, which can be intercepted on the way like any other ([[transfers]]), and your army leaves the city;
- **burn** it — sack it, then raze it to the ground. The city burns on the map for the rest of that game day, for anyone who has eyes on it, and stands as a ruin after. **Nobody may found a city there for 60 game days.**

After **30 game days unchallenged** you are told the city is ripe, and you may also:

- **annex** it — keep it as your own. It becomes one of your cities, never your capital. Ships in its harbour change hands with it.

Until you choose, the city remains occupied.

Make the choice from the dispatch that told you about it — sack/burn/annex are buttons right
there, no need to leave the browser — or from the command line with `keryx occupation` ([[keryx]]).

## Relieving an occupied city {#occupation-when-it-happens-to-you}

You are notified when your city is occupied, when an occupation is broken, and — if it comes to that — when it is sacked, looted, burned or taken. A relief force is your answer: every fight at the city resets the occupier's countdown.

If the city you lose was your last, see [[last-city]].

## Losing your capital {#occupation-capital-succession}

If your capital is annexed, razed or collapses while you still hold another city, your **most populous** remaining city becomes your capital at once; there is no choice to make. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/succession.go handleOwnerCityLoss -->

gods:
The gods are real in Megaron. Their goodwill toward your people is [[kharis]]: kept up by temple workers and daily offerings, lost through neglect. In return they answer prayers ([[rites]]) and send true omens ([[gossip]]).

Each god has their own [[temple|Temple]]. A temple opens that god's prayers in its city; build it again to raise its level, which raises how much kharis your realm can hold ([[temples]]).

## The Minoan gods

<!-- list: god -->
| Name | In short |
|---|---|
| [[potnia]] | Potnia, the Mistress: mother of animals and of the sea. |
| [[velchanos]] | Velchanos, the young god: the bull, the seasons, death and rebirth. He brings the fields back. |
| [[asterion]] | Asterion, lord of the labyrinth. |
| [[sea-daimons]] | The Sea Daimons of Stillness: not persons but forces, wind, wave and the deep. |
<!-- /list -->

The gods do not want to be challenged. A ruler who neglects them meets their wrath ([[kharis]]).
kharis:
**Kharis** is your standing with [[gods|the gods]] — a relationship, not a resource. It is held for your whole realm, not per city, and your [[account|Account]] summary shows its current amount. The **Kult (⛩)** drawer shows the number, mood and its current meaning:

## Divine moods {#kharis-details}

| Mood | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Favorable** (60 and above) | The gods may bless you: a blessed harvest (a quarter more food for 25 game days, [[fish|fish]] excepted) or unexpected recruits. |
| **Indifferent** (30 to below 60) | They have noticed you and do nothing. |
| **Suspicious** (5 to below 30) | Below 15, a 3% chance of punishment each game day, with or without a temple; recent punishment gives seven game days of protection. |
| **Wrathful** (below 5) | The same risk below 15, except during protection: [[war-chariot|chariots]] break, ships are lost, food rots or plague takes a garrison. |

A standing temple and at least **60 kharis** give a **15% chance of a spontaneous blessing each game day**. This is separate from a prayer: kharis is a requirement for prayers, never spent. The number is your standing, not a percentage. Protection temporarily removes punishment risk; a favorable mood without a standing temple cannot bring spontaneous blessings. These are dice rolls, not promises.

### Starting standing and true omens {#kharis-details-2}

Higher kharis also brings true omens more often, from farther away and with more detail. Only the highest standing can rarely point to a concrete place for an urgent fact. Omens never reveal exact strength, future arrival times or routes, and do not reveal unknown place names.

Blessings and punishments arrive as notifications.

A new Wanax starts at **40 Kharis**, before founding. Rising again keeps your standing with the gods, with the floor as a minimum. Kharis never falls all the way to nothing. It fades from the start; founding does not pause decay.

## Maintaining divine standing {#raising-kharis}

Three things must be true, every game day:

1. **You have a temple.** Without one, kharis decays. Each temple belongs to one god, a city may hold one per god, and kharis is still one pool for the realm.
2. **People serve in it** — placed temple workers, 2 workplaces per level in each temple. Each earns 1.05 kharis per game day before the offering factor, scarcity and decay. See [[temples]].
3. **The temple is fed** — each temple's own daily reference gift of 0.25 [[grain|grain]], with local fish, [[timber|timber]] or [[silver|silver]] as substitutes of equal divine value. See [[temples]] for the selection order and planned gift.

In a small realm, a fully staffed, fed level-1 temple can earn more favour than the realm loses each game day. Compare the projected net; a larger realm may need more temples or higher levels. Larger temples can employ more devotion and raise kharis faster when staffed and fed.

### The Kharis ceiling and offerings {#raising-kharis-2}

**Your best temple sets your ceiling:** no temple **40**, level 1 **50**, level 2 **75**, level 3 **100**. Everyday prayers work at a level-1 temple. Spontaneous blessings need **60 kharis** and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts.

Kharis decays every game day regardless. Additional cities and residents increase cult [[upkeep|upkeep]] even when every city has a temple ([[colonies]]).

Kharis is a requirement for [[rites|prayers]], never spent. Everyday prayers answer when their requirements are met; they cost goods and waiting time.

An ongoing **blessed harvest** appears beside Food in the city drawer and in
`keryx status` and `keryx city`, with its yield bonus, affected goods and game days left.
The row disappears when the blessing ends; fish receives no harvest bonus.

The temple shows how much each good counts with the gods, before a particular god's preferences. What the world can spare can raise what devotion earns; this is the gods' reckoning, not a buying price. The ordinary daily offering and your choice of devotion remain separate from a prayer's one-time gift.

### Kult tabs and changes in standing {#raising-kharis-3}

A notification marks each change between **Favorable**, **Indifferent**, **Suspicious** and **Wrathful**, with the new Kharis value and recorded game day. Check **Kult** for decay and temple support; staff and feed your [[temples]].

Demolishing a temple voluntarily costs **10 kharis per level**, with a floor of **1**; plundering causes no such debt. The demolition loss is immediate. A lower ceiling takes no additional kharis; above it, daily cult upkeep lowers kharis and temple workers and offerings do not raise it. The confirmation shows the loss and any ceiling change. See [[temple-demolition]].

The **Kult** drawer has three tabs: **Kharis** for this realm-wide standing and
its daily change, **Prayers** for prayers in each of your cities, and **[[temple|Temples]]**
for every temple's god, city, level, workers and daily gift. Your standing is
shared; an offering still comes from the city named in its prayer row. See
[[temples]] for the controls.

## Divine wrath {#divine-wrath}

The gods may punish a realm **below 15 kharis**, with or without a [[temples|temple]]. Each game day brings a **3% chance**. At exactly 15 there is no risk. A punishment chooses one of your active cities that has something it can take.

### Warnings of divine wrath {#divine-wrath-warning-before-danger}

When your standing crosses **30 downward** and the projected net is negative, a warning tells you your kharis, net per game day and how many game days it would take to reach 15 at that rate. It is sent once per downward crossing. A positive or zero net gives no warning. Further decline below 30 does not repeat it; recovery above 30 allows a new downward crossing to warn again.

The estimate assumes that net continues. Staff and feed your temples, then check **Kult** or `keryx status`. A mood change still has its own notice.

### Protection after punishment {#divine-wrath-seven-game-days-after-punishment}

An actual loss gives your whole realm **seven game days of protection from further divine punishment**. A game day follows this world's pace; **Kult**, `keryx status` and the punishment notice show the protection's end in your local clock. Repeated processing does not extend it. At the end, the ordinary risk resumes if kharis is still below 15. The protection follows the Wanax, across their cities and temples.

If there is nothing to take, there is no punishment and no new protection. Protection does not stop cult upkeep or prevent losses from [[food|hunger]], [[battle|battle]] or weather.

### Temples and divine punishment {#divine-wrath-temple-levels}

Everyday prayers work at a level-1 temple. Spontaneous blessings need **60 kharis** and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts. The ceilings remain **50 / 75 / 100** for temple levels 1 / 2 / 3. See [[kharis]] and [[rites]].
temples:
A **[[temple]]** ([[buildings]]) is how you keep [[gods|the gods]]' favour ([[kharis]]). Every temple is dedicated to **one god**: [[potnia]], [[velchanos]], [[asterion]] or the [[sea-daimons|Sea Daimons]] of Stillness. A city may hold several temples, but **at most one per god**. They are named by their god: Temple of Potnia, Temple of Velchanos, and so on. Each temple needs two things from you.

## Building and upgrading temples {#temples-building-one}

Choose the god when you build. On the web, **City → Construct** lists one row per god; in Keryx, `keryx build --type temple --god potnia`. Building the same god's temple again raises that temple's level. Each prayer is said at its own god's temple ([[rites]]): Potnia's two prayers at Potnia's, [[green-shoots]] at Velchanos's, [[the-thread-shows-a-path]] at Asterion's, [[favourable-passage]] at the Sea Daimons'. Every prayer works from a level-1 temple. Demolishing a temple frees only its own workers.

## Temple workers {#temple-workers}

**City → [[catchment]] & workplaces → Temple**: place or remove whole [[citizens]] with the same controls as other workplaces. In Keryx, use `staff temple +1` or `staff temple -1`; `roster` includes them. When a city has several temples, name the god: `keryx staff temple +1 --god velchanos`. The web shows one card per temple.

Each temple level provides **2 workplaces**: level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 4 and level 3 holds 6. A worker stands at one temple only. These people leave the idle pool, and cannot work another job at the same time. An empty temple has no devotion gain. Founding a city grants no automatic temple staffing.

Each placed temple worker earns **1.05 kharis per game day** before the offering factor, scarcity and realm decay. A fully staffed level-1 temple earns **2.1** before these adjustments. Kult shows local staffing and the projected realm net. <!-- src: server/internal/kharis/tick.go KharisPerTempleWorker -->

## A temple’s daily offering {#daily-offerings}

Each temple has its own daily reference gift of **0.25 [[grain|grain]]**, taken only from its own city's stock. When a city holds several temples, they are planned in god-ID order — Asterion, Potnia, the Sea Daimons of Stillness, Velchanos — each against what the earlier ones left in the store. A temple's workers earn kharis only on game days that temple was fed. Kharis stays one pool for the whole realm. [[fish]], [[timber|timber]] and [[silver|silver]] can replace grain at the same divine value; a gift may combine goods. The amount of a substitute can change with the world's divine values. <!-- src: server/internal/kharis/temple_offering.go TempleOfferingGrain -->

The temple uses **grain first, then fish, then timber, and silver last**. Silver is never required. [[oil]] and [[wine|wine]] are not used for this standing gift; [[rites|prayers]] keep their own offerings.

### Planning temple offerings {#daily-offerings-2}

**Kult → Temple offerings** and `keryx status` show one row per temple with the reference, equivalent alternatives, the stock it would find after earlier temples, and the planned next gift, with a ✓ or ✗. If the city cannot fund the whole gift, nothing is taken and that temple earns no offering gain for the game day. Devotion and the daily decay still determine your net kharis change.

## Temple levels and the Kharis ceiling {#temple-levels}

With full devotion and its daily gift, a level-1 temple can raise kharis in a small realm. Compare its gain with the cost of all your active cities and residents in **Kult → [[upkeep|Upkeep]] of the cult** and the projected net. A temple does not cancel city costs, but it does not protect low standing from [[divine-wrath|divine wrath]]. Higher-level temples can employ more devotion and make it grow faster when staffed and fed.

**Your best temple sets your kharis ceiling:** no temple 40, level 1 50, level 2 75, level 3 100. Everyday prayers work at a level-1 temple. Spontaneous blessings need 60 kharis and a maintained temple. Only a level-2 temple or higher lets kharis grow that far. Kharis retained above a lowered ceiling still counts. Levelling a temple further needs [[cedar|cedar]].

### Temple demolition and realm temple lists {#temple-levels-2}

Demolishing a temple voluntarily costs **10 kharis per level**, with a floor of **1**; plundering causes no such debt. The demolition loss is immediate. A lower ceiling takes no additional kharis; above it, daily cult upkeep lowers kharis and temple workers and offerings do not raise it. The confirmation shows the loss and any ceiling change. See [[temple-demolition]].

## Finding your temples {#temples-find-your-temples}

**Kult → Temples** lists every standing temple in your realm, with its city, god,
level, workers and next daily offering. **Manage in City** opens that temple's
city for staffing or building. Demolition asks for confirmation and shows the
current kharis loss and new ceiling. Temples you have not built are listed last.

**Kult → Prayers** lists prayers across your cities, with the temple and city
where each can be offered. Prayers you can prepare now come first; prayers
whose temples are missing come last. Each Offer uses that row's city and stock.
Gods' waiting times still apply across your realm. **Kult → Kharis** explains your
realm's standing, daily change and current divine risk; see [[kharis]].

`keryx status` lists all your temples. `keryx rite --list` lists prayers across
your realm with the `--settlement` to use for each; add `--settlement <id>` to
filter the list to one city.

## Daily upkeep of the cult {#cult-upkeep}

Daily upkeep is **0.1 base + 0.2 per city beyond the first + 0.1 per 1,000 residents**. It counts all your active cities, including your capital, whether or not they have temples. Sunk, collapsed and razed cities do not count. Residents are the actual population in those cities, including people short of a whole citizen; armies and crews away from the population are not counted a second time. This is the upkeep of the cult, rather than an extra penalty that accelerates as your realm grows.

For **three cities with 2,500 residents altogether**, upkeep is **0.1 + 0.4 + 0.25 = 0.75 kharis per game day**. A realm without a city has the base cost only.

### Temple production and punishment risk {#cult-upkeep-2}

**Kult → Upkeep of the cult** and `keryx status` show the base, cities and residents separately, alongside projected temple production and net. One more fed temple worker gives **at least +1.05 kharis per game day**, and more when the cult’s reference offering of grain is scarce in the world. This describes the extra worker's yield: employing one also requires a free citizen, an available temple workplace and that temple's daily offering. A temple earns favour; it does not remove its city's cost.

Below **15 Kharis**, there is a 3% chance of punishment each game day **with or without a temple**. An actual punishment gives **seven game days of protection**. A game day follows this world's pace; Kult and `keryx status` show the protection's end in your local clock. Nothing taken means no new protection. See [[divine-wrath]]. A punishment chooses a random eligible city of yours with something it can take; it need not strike the capital.

## Demolishing a temple {#temple-demolition}

Voluntarily demolishing a [[temples|temple]] angers its god. Your realm loses **10 kharis per temple level**, down to a **floor of 1**. This is an immediate consequence of your own demolition, separate from the daily chance of [[divine-wrath|divine punishment]]. It does not grant punishment protection.

Before you confirm, **City → Demolish** and `keryx demolish --type temple --god potnia` show the actual kharis loss, standing afterward and the ceiling before and after. Keryx asks for confirmation; non-interactive or `--json` use without `--yes` previews the consequences without demolishing. Run again with `--yes` to confirm. The result and the **god is angered** notification record what actually happened. Nothing is refunded, and only that temple's workers become idle.

Your best remaining temple determines the ceiling: no temple **40**, level 1 **50**, level 2 **75**, level 3 **100**. Another equally high temple can keep the ceiling unchanged. **Demolition costs kharis immediately; the lower ceiling takes no additional kharis.** Standing above it declines by ordinary daily cult upkeep; temple gains do not offset this decline. Once standing is at or below the ceiling, ordinary gain and upkeep apply again. The voluntary demolition loss still applies.

A temple destroyed by **plundering** creates **no demolition debt** for its owner. Its loss can lower the ceiling and remove its production. Cancelling construction is not demolition and does not incur the kharis loss.
rites:
A rite is a request made at the temple of its god.

A **rite** is a request to [[gods|the gods]]. Open **Kult → Prayers**.

Each prayer is said at its own god's [[temples|temple]], so a city needs that temple standing: [[potnias-vision]] and [[mistress-of-the-walls]] need a [[temple]] of [[potnia]], [[green-shoots]] a Temple of [[velchanos]], [[the-thread-shows-a-path]] a Temple of [[asterion]], [[favourable-passage]] a Temple of the [[sea-daimons|Sea Daimons]] of Stillness. Level 1 is enough. Without it the prayer shows "no Temple of …".

## Temples required by prayers {#rites-details}

Each prayer names its god, the minimum standing it needs, and its traditional offering. Press **Offer**: a row opens with a field for each good, filled with the prayer's recipe. Bring it as it stands, or change the numbers first.

## Standing and offerings for prayers {#prayer-requirements}

**[[kharis]] is never spent on a prayer.** Each of the five Minoan everyday prayers answers when you meet its standing requirement, have its god's temple, and can bring its offering. Waiting time, an active gift or an unused departure gift can still prevent a new prayer.

Bring the traditional recipe or a composed offering worth at least as much to that god. If you lack the traditional gift, **Compose offering** opens empty fields so you can choose other goods you hold. Choose some goods before bringing the gift. `keryx rite --list` marks this as **compose**; use `rite --offer good=amount` to choose the gift. In an interactive terminal, Keryx shows your chosen goods and exact amounts before asking **Cast?**; answering no leaves the gift untouched. A smaller gift is refused without taking goods. Bringing more does not improve the answer. For these prayers, `--offer-multiplier` is ignored; omitting a composed offering always brings the traditional recipe.

### Waiting between prayers {#prayer-requirements-2}

An answered prayer starts that god's waiting time across all your cities. **Kult** and `keryx rite --list` show the remaining wait, an active gift or a gift awaiting departure. Missing temples and insufficient kharis are named as separate requirements. Potnia's two prayers share her 24-game day wait. An active gift cannot be renewed before it ends. A gift awaiting departure cannot be renewed before it is used.

Older prayers outside the current Minoan catalogue retain their uncertain answer and offering multiplier. Their offering is spent even on a silent answer, but kharis is never spent. Old recorded outcomes remain as they happened.

## Prayer answers and active blessings {#rites-the-prayers}

The current Minoan prayers are **Potnia's Vision**, **Mistress of the Walls**, **Green Shoots**, **The Thread Shows a Path** and **Favourable Passage**, described below. `keryx rite --list` or **Kult → Prayers** shows the prayers your culture can offer and why one is unavailable. Current kharis is shown with a decimal; eligibility uses the exact pool value.

The answer or a refusal appears in the Kult drawer after you offer; it stays beside the prayers. An answer also arrives as a dispatch naming the god, the prayer and what was granted. When the god marks a place, **⌖ Take me there** goes to it. In Keryx it is listed by `keryx notifications`.

An ongoing **blessed harvest** appears beside Food in the city drawer and in
`keryx status` and `keryx city`, with its yield bonus, affected goods and game days left.
The row disappears when the blessing ends; [[fish|fish]] receives no harvest bonus.

## The current Minoan prayers {#minoan-prayers}

- **Potnia's Vision** — offer 10 [[grain|grain]] + 3 [[silver|silver]]. Potnia marks one source of [[copper|copper]], [[tin|tin]], silver or incense you neither see nor remember, and unknown ground within two hexes, as grey memory. It creates no living eyes and shows no moving activity. Potnia waits 24 game days after answering.
- **Mistress of the Walls** — offer 8 grain + 4 [[timber|timber]]. Potnia strengthens your own garrison defending this city by a quarter for 6 game days. It helps neither an attacking army nor soldiers away from that city. It shares Vision's wait.
- **Green Shoots** — offer 15 grain + 2 silver. Velchanos raises grain, [[oil|oil]] and [[wine|wine]] yield by a quarter for 25 game days. Fish and the herd are unchanged. He waits 25 game days after answering.

### Departure prayers {#minoan-prayers-2}

- **The Thread Shows a Path** — offer 4 timber + 3 silver to Asterion. The next land [[transfers|caravan]] or [[runners|Runner]] leaving this city takes a quarter less time on its outward leg. A land caravan can be intercepted only within one hex of an enemy army, instead of two. Runners remain sacred. Asterion waits 12 game days after answering.
- **Favourable Passage** — offer 6 fish + 3 silver to The Sea Daimons of Stillness. The next ship leaving this city takes a quarter less time and suffers no [[storms|storm]] damage on its outward leg. A Runner aboard travels at that ship's actual speed. The Sea Daimons wait 12 game days after answering.

Vision, [[walls|Walls]] and the two departure prayers require at least 5 kharis; Green Shoots requires 30. The temple's ordinary daily offering is separate.

### Gifts awaiting departure {#minoan-prayers-3}

A departure gift stays in the city where you offered until an eligible journey physically leaves. It is used once. It cannot follow the city to a new owner, change a journey already underway, or bless a return leg. **Awaiting next departure** appears beside the prayer while the gift is unused; the god's waiting time is shown separately. Other ongoing gifts show their remaining game days.

In Keryx, `rite --list` shows your prayers, their effects, offerings, active game days, pending departure gifts and waiting time. `rite --prayer <id>` chooses one. Omitting the ID uses the prayer marked as the culture's default — Mistress of the Walls for Minoans.

## The value of an offering {#offerings}

[[bronze|Bronze]] can weigh far more with the gods than grain. The temple shows their current reckoning: how much each good counts before a particular god's preferences. What the world can spare and what the god favours both change an offering's meaning. **Kult** and `keryx rite --list` show these values beside your prayers.

These are offering values. Wanaxes agree their own trade prices. You may compose an offering in the Offer row on the web, or in Keryx with `rite --offer good=amount,...`. Each god has a taste, and the row tells you what this god favours and roughly what it expects. The traditional recipe always suffices.

Any good may be offered. **Wine and oil** are offerings like any other — oil is also food, so do not give up what a hungry city needs. **Incense** is a valuable gift ([[incense]]). For everyday prayers it can help meet the offering requirement; excess value does not improve the answer.
colonies:
Beyond your metropolis you may hold more settlements — up to **five** in all. <!-- src: server/internal/province/training.go MaxSettlementsPerWanax -->

## Founding a colony {#colonies-founding-a-colony}

Right-click the site, select **Found a new settlement on arrival**, [[naming-the-land|name it]], choose the unit, and **March →**. Or left-click empty land and press **Colonize →**. You get the same [[catchment]] forecast as when you [[founding|founded]] your first city.

**The unit is consumed.** Those men become the colony's population — a cohort of 100 founds a colony of 100, and nobody else comes with them. You cannot recall them and you cannot change your mind. To make a colony bigger, march more men there and [[units|disband]] them: they settle as [[citizens|citizens]].

**They carry a colony purse.** The fixed purse comes from the city they leave: **30 [[silver|silver]] for [[spearmen|spearmen]], 60 for [[elite-infantry]], 90 for [[war-chariot|chariots]]**. It becomes the colony's starting silver, independently of daily pay. A colony's spearmen draw no daily silver; professionals and ships still need pay ([[upkeep]]). Send more with a [[transfers|transfer]] when it needs it. Sent from a city with too little, they take what there is, and the order tells you how much short they are. A purse that never reaches a new colony comes back to whichever of your cities the men walk into. <!-- src: server/internal/combat/march_start.go colonistPurse -->

### Reaching a new colony {#colonies-founding-a-colony-2}

You are notified when the colony is founded, with how its food looks.

## Colonies and metropolises {#colonies-colonies-are-not-metropolises}

There is no free starter [[farm]]. If the ground cannot feed them, you must — by [[transfers|transfer]] or a [[routes|standing order]] — until they stand on their own. A colony on a rich mineral site with no farmland is a real strategy, but only if you have already built the [[grain|grain]] route that keeps it alive.

Every active city, including your capital, counts toward [[kharis|upkeep of the cult]], even with a temple. Daily upkeep is 0.1 base + 0.2 per city beyond the first + 0.1 per 1,000 residents across those cities. This supplies the realm's cult; it is not an accelerating expansion penalty. Sunk, collapsed and razed cities do not count. Check the realm breakdown in **Kult** or `keryx status` before expanding.

## Abandoning a colony {#colonies-abandoning-a-colony}

Open **War → Recruit → Abandon settlement**, choose the colony and press **Abandon**. The confirmation appears in the same row: press **Abandon** there to give it up, or **Keep settlement** to cancel. This cannot be undone. In Keryx, use `abandon --settlement <settlement-id>`.

You can abandon only an active colony you own. **Your capital cannot be abandoned.** The colony leaves your realm, its garrison is disbanded, and troops aboard ships in that garrison are disbanded too. Its people do not move to your capital. The ground becomes open for founding again, and you regain a settlement slot.

After confirmation, the colony disappears from your owned settlements. Keryx names the colony you gave up; the web map and settlement list refresh. Abandoning is a peaceful withdrawal.

Founding adds no grain to the colony's stores. Produce food or send it by [[transfers|internal transfer]]; the starting silver is only the carried purse.
bronze:
This is the strategic shape of the whole world.

Bronze needs **[[copper|copper]] and [[tin|tin]]**. **Copper and tin are never found on the same landmass** — the world is made that way on purpose, every time. It is not bad luck, and no new world will fix it.

Therefore **nobody can make bronze alone.** Not the richest Wanax, not the luckiest start. Bronze — and with it [[elite-infantry]], [[war-chariot|chariots]], [[war-galley|war galleys]] and the best walls — exists only for those who cross water, or who trade with someone who has.

## Three roads

1. **[[mine]] one half and buy the other.** The merchant's road, and the most common ([[trade]]).
2. **Sail and found a colony on the other metal's landmass.** Expensive, slow, permanent ([[sea]], [[colonies]]).
3. **Take it from someone carrying it.** A [[transfers|caravan]] of tin crossing your ground is a target ([[stances]]).

Then smelt it: a **[[foundry]]** turns copper and tin into bronze ([[buildings]]).

## If you cannot find copper at all

Go and look — that is what the world is for. Every ship and every scout widens the map ([[sight]]). And you can ask the **oracle** ([[rites]]): it reveals a deposit somewhere you have never been. Getting there is up to you.
report:
Megaron is being built while you play it. When something is wrong, the most useful thing you can do is tell us — from inside the game.

Open **Report (✎)** and choose:

- **Bug — something is broken**,
- **Design — this feels wrong**, or
- **Confused — I don't understand this**.

Tell us what you tried, what you expected and what happened, then press **Send**. Your position on the map, the current game day and what you were looking at are attached automatically, so you do not need to describe them.

A *Confused* report is as valuable as a bug. If this Codex did not answer your question, that is worth a report too.

Before reporting, glance at [[rough-edges]] — it may already be known.

## Things that work, but awkwardly

- **March in the Forces tab takes typed coordinates**, not a map click. Right-clicking the map is the friendlier path — it also reaches forces already on the march ([[marching]]).

**Kingdoms** — formal alliances, elected leaders, shared armies — are built but switched off, and will return once the foundations are proven. For now, diplomacy is [[messengers|letters]] and [[trade]].

keryx:
**Keryx** is Megaron's command-line client — the herald. It talks to the same server as the browser and can do everything a Wanax can do, including a few things the browser cannot do yet ([[rough-edges]]).

You do not need it to play. It exists for players who prefer a terminal, for automation, and for AI players. See [[ai-agents]] for the play rules.

## Setting up Keryx {#keryx-getting-started}

Keryx is a single program; ask whoever runs your world for a copy. Then:

```
export POLEIA_SERVER=https://megaron.formatet.se
keryx login --username <your name>
keryx join
keryx status
```

`keryx actions` is the command to reach for when you are stuck: it lists what you can do right now. `keryx --help`, and `--help` after any command, explain the rest. The rules themselves are in this Codex: `keryx codex` lists the articles and `keryx codex <id>` prints one.

## Common Keryx commands {#keryx-a-few-useful-commands}

```
keryx status                 # your realm at a glance
keryx codex bronze           # read a Codex article
keryx notifications          # the archive — what happened while you were away
keryx notifications --all    # every kind, each event shown separately (latest 100)
keryx dispatches             # which kinds of news are pushed to you live
keryx map                    # the map around you
keryx city                   # people and placement in a city
keryx goods                  # stock and production
keryx password               # change your password
keryx occupation order ...   # sack, burn or annex an occupied city
```

`notifications --all` includes the historical kinds normally hidden or grouped in the default feed. It shows the latest 100 notifications; combine it with `--unread` for unread rows only. It does not mark anything read. Use `--kind` or `--exclude` separately to select kinds.

Orders given through Keryx obey the same rules as in the browser: they travel by [[runners|Runner]] and take game days ([[time]]).

`POLEIA_CONFIG` selects a separate configuration file. `POLEIA_SERVER` and `POLEIA_TOKEN` override connection settings. Command failures show the error and a pointer to `keryx <command> --help`. March previews call the soldiers' [[silver|silver]] cost **Pay**.

### World and city selectors in Keryx {#keryx-a-few-useful-commands-2}

With exactly one active world, commands select and save it automatically. To choose explicitly, run `keryx worlds` and then `keryx worlds --select <world-id>`. City rows show both the placement number and `(q,r)`; use those coordinates with `build --hex q,r`.

Use a city name or province ID either positionally or with `--province` in `city`, `placements`, `status` and `build`. For placement: `keryx place Knossos fish 13 -1` or `keryx place --province Knossos fish 13 -1`. Put flags before the good when using a negative amount. If no [[citizens|citizens]] work that good on the chosen hex, the result lists where they do work it. `founding settle --yes` skips the question. Travel estimates use game days; if an arrival cannot be calculated it is reported as unavailable.

Hex selection accepts the ordinal shown by City, with or without `#`: `build --type lumbermill --hex 6` or `--hex '#6'`. Placement can use `place fish 6 +1`, `place fish '#6' +1`, or `place --hex 6 fish +1`; `--hex q,r` also works. Put flags before the good when giving a negative amount. `staff` is for city workplaces; hex-bound buildings are worked with `place` on their hex.

## Keryx argument syntax {#keryx-argument-reminders}

Start construction with `keryx build --type harbour`. A positional argument in `build`
is the **city**, as in `keryx build Knossos --type harbour`; it is not the building type.
Use `build --list` for the catalogue or `build --queue` for queued construction.

`keryx staff olive_press` shows that named workplace's staffing. Add `+1` or `-1`
to change it; the building name is required. Use `keryx city` or `keryx roster`
to find workplaces and assignments. Hex buildings use `place`.

Send a report with `keryx report --text "what happened"`; use `--kind confused`
for a question the rules did not answer. For [[colonies|colony]] founding in scripts, add
`--yes`: `keryx unit march --unit <id> --target 5,-3 --intent colonize --name Thapsos --yes`.
Without confirmation, the non-interactive text command only shows the forecast;
JSON callers receive a refusal until they add `--yes`.

To learn what a contacted city needs or can spare, ask its Wanax with `keryx messenger` and read the reply with `keryx inbox`. See [[messengers]] and [[trade]].

### Keryx staffing and labour commands {#keryx-argument-reminders-2}

[[temple]] workers use the same citizen pool as other jobs. Use `keryx staff temple +1` to assign one, `staff temple -1` to free one (with several temples, add `--god <god>`), and `roster` to see their assignments. See [[temples]].

Join the [Megaron Discord](https://discord.gg/NxtftQUMYW) for questions, stories and alpha news. The chat is optional and outside the game; send in-world letters through [[messengers]].

## Joining Discord {#community-chat-your-chat-account}

Use your Discord account to join. It is separate from your Megaron account.

## Community rules and privacy {#community-chat-chat-rules-and-privacy}

- Be decent. No harassment, no hate, nothing illegal.
- Talk about the game, not other players’ private lives.
- Keep personal information private.
- Contact a moderator if something in the community needs attention.

Discord is a separate service with its own account and privacy settings. For a problem inside the game, use [[report]].
glossary:
**Catchment** — the land a settlement works: its own hex and the ring within two steps. See [[catchment]].

**Citizen** — one marker on the placement grid; one hundred people. See [[citizens]].

**Contact** — the permanent right to write to and trade with a city, earned by reaching it. See [[contact]].

**[[emporos]]** — a merchant ship. See [[sea]].

**Kharis** — your realm’s standing with [[gods|the gods]]. A new Wanax starts at 40; it fades from the start, with a daily cost that grows with your active cities and their residents. See [[kharis]].

**Kult** — the drawer for the gods and the temple.

**Metropolis** — your first city, founded from the Nomadic Host. See [[founding]].

**Nomadic Host** — the people you begin as, before you found a city. See [[horde]].

**Runner** — the person who carries your order to a unit in the field. See [[runners]].

**Sentry** — the watch stance; also how a [[sieges|siege]] is laid. See [[stances]].

**Food coverage** — how long the city’s [[grain|grain]], [[fish|fish]] and [[oil|oil]] stocks last at current consumption. See [[food]].

**Standing order** — a [[transfers|caravan]] route that runs by itself. See [[routes]].

**The Thalassa** — the sea. See [[sea]].

**game day** — the world’s unit of time; the calendar names its date. See [[time]].

**Wanax** — a ruler; you. See [[welcome]].

market:
A Market gives your city a **market board**: one line saying what the city buys and one saying what it sells, up to three goods each. You write it yourself, and it says only what you choose. Nothing checks it against your stores, and it can be empty.

Other rulers read the board on the spot. Their [[transfers|caravans]], armies and ships read it when they pass within reach of the market, and their [[messengers|messengers]] read it when they arrive in the city. A level 1 Market reaches as far as the city's own fields, and each higher level reaches further. What they read stays with their ruler as it stood then. If you change the board later, they see the change only the next time someone of theirs passes.

A ruler whose caravan reads your board from a distance learns where your city lies. They can write to you, but before they can send you a [[trade|trade offer]] their own people must reach the city. The board does not trade for you; it tells others whom to ask.

Write it in **City → Buildings → Market board**, or with `keryx market-board <city> --buys tin --sells wine`. The Market needs no workers.

Build or upgrade it in **City → Buildings → Construct**, or use `keryx build --type market`.
